NoteShort on time?



MAFFT takes roughly 2-3 minutes on 114 sequences this size (longer if you fetched more than 100): a good moment to answer the questions above if you have not already, or read ahead. If it fails or does not finish, skip straight to the trimming step below using the prepared sars_variants_aligned.fasta, already in your data folder from block A, in place of your own sars_variants_aligned_mine.fasta.


An alignment this size, built from real, un-curated submissions, is a good candidate for a quality check before you trust it with a tree: a handful of columns are usually mostly gaps or ambiguous bases for one or two sequences, adding noise rather than real signal. ClipKIT finds and trims columns like that automatically. It is not a cluster module (there is none), so you install it once into your own account, the same way you would on your own laptop:
module purge
module load Python
python3 -m pip install --user clipkit
~/.local/bin/clipkit ../results/sars_variants_aligned_mine.fasta -m smart-gap -o ../results/sars_variants_trimmed_mine.fasta
Four lines, four different jobs. module purge unloads MAFFT and everything it pulled in, so it cannot clash with the Python module you are about to load — a precaution worth taking whenever you switch from one cluster tool to an unrelated one in the same session. module load Python gives you python3 and, bundled with it, pip, Python’s own installer (the bare system python3 on LEGcompute does not have pip, which is why this module matters). python3 -m pip install --user clipkit means “run the pip module through this Python, and install the package named clipkit”; --user installs it into your own account (~/.local/bin) instead of a shared system location you do not have permission to write to. That last part is also why the final line spells out ~/.local/bin/clipkit in full instead of just clipkit: the shell only looks for bare command names in a specific list of folders, $PATH, and your new ~/.local/bin is not on that list — spelling out exactly where the program is sidesteps the question entirely, the same way ./script.sh or a full path works for any program regardless of $PATH. (If you ever see others fix this with export PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH instead, that adds the folder to the search list rather than naming the file directly — same result, but only inside that one terminal tab, which is an easy thing to lose track of if you switch tabs partway through.) Finally, clipkit input -m smart-gap -o output: -m smart-gap picks the trimming mode described above, -o names the output file explicitly instead of letting ClipKIT invent one by appending .clipkit to the input name.






NoteCheckpoint



The install takes a few seconds the first time (downloads clipkit and two small dependencies from PyPI, nothing to do with NCBI or micromamba). ClipKIT itself finishes in under a second and prints a short report: original alignment length, how many sites it trimmed, and the percentage. On this alignment, expect it to trim around 1% of columns — a small, reassuring number: most of what you downloaded was already usable, this step is a safety check, not a rescue. It writes one output file, the trimmed alignment you named above with -o.


module load FastTree
FastTree -nt ../results/sars_variants_trimmed_mine.fasta > ../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk






NoteCheckpoint



FastTree takes under a minute even on 114 sequences this size: it is approximate by design, the same trade-off from the theory block. ../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk now holds 114 tips instead of five, each internal split labelled with its own support value, not a uniform 1.000 like the small worked example from blocks B-D2.


Now plot it. plot_tree.R reads ../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk, roots it on unknown_sample (a real outgroup this time, not a SARS-CoV-2 genome itself), and labels the 13 named variants and unknown_sample in colour; the other 100 tips stay thin and grey, real background diversity rather than something to identify. Open the script in the Source editor and read it top to bottom before running anything. Widen the Plots pane first (drag its border, or maximise it): 114 tips need more vertical room than five did.






ImportantThe Console has its own working directory



Session 1 told you the Console is a different panel from the Terminal; it also has a different working directory, one that does not follow the cd commands you have been typing in the Terminal all session. source("plot_tree.R") runs in the Console, so it looks for plot_tree.R wherever the Console currently is, not wherever the Terminal is — if that is not your data folder, you get cannot open file 'plot_tree.R': No such file or directory, even though the file is really there.
Fix it once, in the Console: in the Files pane (bottom right), click into bioinfo_course/session_03/data, then More → Set As Working Directory. Confirm it worked with getwd() in the Console — it should print that same path. Then run source("plot_tree.R") again.


source("plot_tree.R")






NoteCheckpoint



Some crowding near the top is normal at this tip count; it clears up once you export at a larger size (next step). Three things to confirm: first, unknown_sample sits on a branch far longer than any other, dozens of times longer than a typical branch between two SARS-CoV-2 genomes — it is related to the rest of the tree, but clearly not one of them, the same conclusion blocks B-D2 reached by a completely different method. Second, the Omicron sublineages (BA.1 through 24C) should all fall within one connected part of the tree, separate from the earlier named variants (Alpha, Delta, Gamma, Mu) — consistent with Omicron descending from a single common ancestor. Third, Delta should be the named variant branching closest to Wuhan-Hu-1, before Mu, Alpha, Gamma, and Omicron.




3.3.7 What rooting actually does, and why this edit matters
FastTree does not know which end of the tree is “the start”: it only works out how closely everything is related to everything else, the branching pattern itself. That branching pattern on its own can be drawn equally validly starting from any point — rooting is choosing one tip or node and saying “draw the tree growing out from here.” Changing the root never changes which tips are each other’s closest relatives; it only changes which one ends up treated as the single outlier versus everything else. This is exactly the outgroup idea from the theory block’s glossary, now something you do yourself instead of just reading a definition: a good root is a sequence you have independent reason to believe sits outside the group you are actually comparing, so that everything else is free to arrange itself by real relatedness, undistorted by the choice of root. unknown_sample is a good root precisely because blocks B-D2 already gave you independent evidence it is not a SARS-CoV-2 variant at all.


3.3.8 How to make the edit

Open plot_tree.R in the Source editor (top-left pane): click its tab if it is already open, or double-click the file in the Files pane if not.
Find this line, a little below library(ape) and the read.tree(...) line:
root_on <- "unknown_sample"
<- is R’s assignment operator (“store the thing on the right in the name on the left”): this line stores the text "unknown_sample" in a variable called root_on, which the very next line (tree <- root(tree, outgroup = root_on, ...)) then uses.
Click right between the quotation marks and retype the accession, so the line reads:
root_on <- "MN908947.1"
Keep the quotation marks: root_on holds a piece of text, not a number or a bare word.
Save the file (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S, or the editor’s Save icon) before doing anything else. This is the step people most often skip: if you do not save, source() below re-runs the old, unedited file from disk, and nothing about your plot changes, even though the editor shows your new text.
Switch to the Console (bottom-left pane, not the Terminal) and run source("plot_tree.R") again, exactly as before — or click the Source button at the top of the editor pane, which does the same thing without you needing to type anything in the Console.







NoteCheckpoint



The named variants still group with each other exactly as before — that part is the point, and it holds regardless of what the plot looks like. On this particular tree, the two plots will look almost identical, close enough that you may need to look twice to tell them apart: Wuhan-Hu-1’s own branch is nearly zero length (you can check this in ../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk, right next to its name), so it sits essentially at the point everything else branches from either way — rooting there or rooting just outside it, on unknown_sample, lands in almost the same place visually. That is a real result, not a sign that your edit failed: if source() ran with no error and the Console shows no leftover red text, the reroot worked, whether or not you can see it.
Change root_on back to "unknown_sample" now (edit, save, source() again) — unknown_sample is the correct root and the version you submit; the MN908947.1 version was only for this comparison, not something to export or hand in.


Export the figure: in the Plots pane, Export → Save as Image… (or Save as PDF…), into results/. Any format the dialog offers is fine to submit (PNG, JPEG, SVG, PDF, …): Moodle accepts all of them, there is no single required file type here. Set the height generously, at least 14 inches (or ~1400 px) if you are offered a choice: 114 labelled and unlabelled tips need the extra room to stay legible, more than the on-screen preview shows. This tree image is today’s required figure for block D.






NoteShort on time?



If the fetch, MAFFT, or FastTree did not finish, change the file name near the top of plot_tree.R from "../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk" to "sars_variants_tree.nwk", the prepared fallback copied in block A, and continue from there.


In Section 4 of WORKSHEET.md, write a few sentences describing your tree image, the same way you would in a lab notebook: where unknown_sample sits and how its branch compares to the rest; whether the named variants fall in the order you would expect; and, using the collection date you looked up earlier, to what era do most of your 100 background sequences most likely belong — recent, or as old as the earliest named variants? (Hint: check a handful of background headers in sars_variants.fasta with grep ">" sars_variants.fasta | head, and compare the years you see there to MN908947.1’s collection date.) The image file itself is submitted alongside WORKSHEET.md, not pasted into it.
If you have more time: unknown_sample is the longest branch by far, but it is not the only one worth a second look — among the 100 background sequences, one or two are still noticeably longer than most. Real NCBI submissions are not curated the way today’s other files are: what might explain a real sequence standing out like that (a sequencing or assembly error, a genuinely unusual isolate, a mislabelled sample)? There is no single correct answer; this is the kind of judgement call real analyses require.
Continue this before Thursday if you do not get to it in class. Your 114-tip tree above, with unknown_sample rooted as an outgroup, stays your main, required result for block D — nothing below replaces it or needs redoing it. This next part asks a different kind of question with the same real data.
A tree is a summary: it compresses an entire alignment, every column of every sequence, down into a branching diagram of who is related to whom. That compression is exactly what makes a 114-tip tree readable at all — but it also means you never actually see the alignment it was built from. Block C had you do this by eye, counting mismatches column by column, but only for a 60-column window of five sequences; at 114 sequences and tens of thousands of columns, counting by hand is no longer possible, and even a colour-coded view would be too dense to read. The 13 named variants, on their own, are small enough to both align and genuinely look at, the same way block C did, just with a proper tool doing the counting instead of your own eyes.
Fetch the 13 named variants again, this time into their own file, separate from the 100 background genomes. module purge from the ClipKIT and FastTree steps above unloaded EntrezDirect along with everything else, so load it again first — if you see efetch: command not found without this line, this is why:
module purge
module load EntrezDirect
efetch -db nuccore -id MN908947.1,MW931310.1,OU297363.1,OK252993.1,MZ727692.1,OX315743.1,OX315675.1,OP093374.1,OP164778.1,OP457109.1,PP997352.1,PQ325441.1,PQ356432.1 -format fasta > sars_named_variants.fasta
Their headers are the same long NCBI descriptions as before (>MN908947.1 Wuhan seafood market pneumonia virus isolate Wuhan-Hu-1, complete genome, and so on) — fine for a computer to match on the accession, but unreadable as labels in a viewer. Replace each with a short name using sed, a search-and-replace command you have not used yet today: sed 's/PATTERN/REPLACEMENT/' file searches each line of file for PATTERN and swaps in REPLACEMENT; -i makes it edit the file in place instead of printing the result to the screen. >MN908947.1.* matches the whole header line starting with that accession (. means “any character”, * means “zero or more of the previous thing”, so .* means “the rest of the line, whatever it is”), and >Wuhan_China replaces all of it. One sed line per accession, 13 lines total, each one only touching its own header:
sed -i "s/>MN908947.1.*/>Wuhan_China/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>MW931310.1.*/>Delta_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OU297363.1.*/>Alpha_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OK252993.1.*/>Gamma_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>MZ727692.1.*/>Mu_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OX315743.1.*/>Omicron_BA.1_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OX315675.1.*/>Omicron_BA.2_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OP093374.1.*/>Omicron_BA.4_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OP164778.1.*/>Omicron_BA.5_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>OP457109.1.*/>Omicron_BA.2.75_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>PP997352.1.*/>Omicron_24A_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>PQ325441.1.*/>Omicron_24B_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
sed -i "s/>PQ356432.1.*/>Omicron_24C_variant/" sars_named_variants.fasta
grep ">" sars_named_variants.fasta






NoteCheckpoint



13 short, readable headers, one per named variant. Each sed line only matches its own accession, so the order you run them in does not matter.


Align these 13 on their own, then trim with ClipKIT again, the same two tools and the same smart-gap mode as above, just on much less data: MAFFT finishes in roughly 11 seconds instead of two and a half minutes, not a better result, just less data to compare pairwise.
module load MAFFT
mafft --auto --thread 8 sars_named_variants.fasta > sars_named_variants_aligned.fasta
module purge
module load Python
python3 -m pip install --user clipkit
~/.local/bin/clipkit sars_named_variants_aligned.fasta -m smart-gap






NoteCheckpoint



pip install finishes almost instantly this time: ClipKIT is already installed in your account from earlier in this block. On 13 sequences, expect a somewhat higher percentage of columns trimmed than the ~1% on the full 114 (roughly double, in testing) — with far fewer sequences to vote on whether a column is “real,” a handful of genuinely gappy positions make up a bigger share of the whole alignment. This writes one output file, sars_named_variants_aligned.fasta.clipkit.


Download sars_named_variants_aligned.fasta.clipkit to your computer (Files pane → select it → More → Export), then open EBI’s alignment viewer, choose DNA as the input type, and upload it. After about a minute, you get back exactly what block C showed you in miniature: rows of sequences, columns of aligned positions, except now it is all ~29,787 columns and all 13 named variants at once, each base coloured by identity. Scroll across it: wide, uniformly-coloured stretches are columns where every variant agrees (the vast majority of the genome, since these are all the same virus species); the stretches where colours break up are exactly the positions carrying the mutations that define one variant from another, the same kind of difference you counted one by one in block C’s 60-column window, now visible across the whole genome at a glance.
In Section 4 of WORKSHEET.md: does any one region of the genome look more variable across the 13 variants than the rest, by eye? Do the Omicron sublineages’ columns look more similar to each other than to Wuhan_China’s, consistent with what the big tree already showed you?
For more SARS-CoV-2 data than you could reasonably fetch by hand today, including how these and many other variants actually spread over time and place, see Nextstrain — no setup required, just a browser.


3.3.9 D2. The same question, at the protein level (16:40-16:50, pairs)
reference_spike_proteins.fasta holds the same four coronaviruses’ spike proteins, including the exact Session 1 record, SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1 (UniProt P0DTC2). Build a protein database and search the file against itself. BLAST+ was loaded back in block B, but block D’s module purge steps (for ClipKIT, for FastTree) unloaded it along with everything else, so load it again first — if makeblastdb/blastp come back as “command not found”, this is why:
module purge
module load BLAST+
makeblastdb -in reference_spike_proteins.fasta -dbtype prot -out ../results/protein_db
blastp -query reference_spike_proteins.fasta -db ../results/protein_db -max_hsps 1 -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid pident length evalue bitscore" -out ../results/blastp_result.tsv
cat ../results/blastp_result.tsv
Each sequence is searched against all four, including itself, so ignore the self-hits (pident 100: a sequence always matches itself perfectly).






NoteCheckpoint



blastp_result.tsv has 16 lines: four references, each searched against all four (including itself), one best match per pair. Find the line pairing SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1 with SARS-CoV-1_Tor2: percent identity at the protein level. Compare it with the same pair’s percent identity at the nucleotide level, from block B’s deep search (blast_result_deep.tsv). Protein identity comes out a little higher. Several different DNA codons can encode the same amino acid: a nucleotide substitution that lands on one of those “silent” positions changes the gene without changing the protein. Write this comparison, with both numbers, in Section 4 of your worksheet.




3.3.10 E. Draft your interpretation; submit on Moodle by Thursday (16:50-17:00)
Start this alone, in Section 5 of WORKSHEET.md. You now have four required kinds of evidence about unknown_sample: the quick BLAST hit, the deep BLAST table, the alignment and distance table, and the protein-level check. Block D’s 114-tip tree is a fifth, bonus piece of evidence: unknown_sample’s unusually long branch, apart from all 113 real SARS-CoV-2 genomes, is a strong, independent confirmation, by a completely different method, of the same conclusion. Citing it strengthens an answer but is not required. Write:

a conclusion answering today’s biological question for unknown_sample, citing evidence from at least two of the four required sources by name (block D’s tree can count as a bonus third or more);
one sentence naming a limitation, uncertainty, or assumption in today’s analysis (the block B/C disagreement over MERS-CoV versus HCoV-OC43_seasonal is one honest candidate, but not the only one).

Get a complete draft down before you leave; a clear, unrushed final version, in your own words, is due on Moodle by Thursday.


3.3.11 Wrap-up
Save your script, confirm results/ contains both BLAST tables, blastp_result.tsv, sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk, and your exported tree image. Submit WORKSHEET.md plus the tree image through Moodle by Thursday: any file format works for the image (PNG, JPEG, PDF, SVG, …), and WORKSHEET.md can be submitted as-is (plain text/Markdown) or converted to PDF or Word first if you prefer — Moodle accepts any of these, there is no required file type beyond “readable.”

3.5 Optional challenge
For your own interest, not graded.
A. Root on a background tip instead. In plot_tree.R, set root_on to one of the unlabelled background accessions instead of unknown_sample (grep ">" sars_variants.fasta for options). Does this change the named variants’ grouping at all? Why might rooting on unknown_sample (as the script does by default, confirmed as a real outgroup by its long branch and by blocks B-D2) give a more defensible picture than rooting on an arbitrary background sequence, even though both are valid trees mathematically?
B. A distance correction model. Today’s small tree (blocks B-D2) used raw percent difference as its distance. Try a correction model that accounts for multiple substitutions at the same site:
library(ape)
aln <- read.dna("aligned_spike.fasta", format = "fasta")
d_raw <- dist.dna(aln, model = "raw", pairwise.deletion = TRUE)
d_jc <- dist.dna(aln, model = "JC69", pairwise.deletion = TRUE)
round(as.matrix(d_raw)["unknown_sample", ] * 100, 1)
round(as.matrix(d_jc)["unknown_sample", ] * 100, 1)
The closest reference barely moves under the correction; the two most distant ones move a lot more. Given the “saturation” idea from the theory block, why would correction matter more for distant pairs than for close ones? (FastTree’s own log, printed to the screen each time you ran it today, names the distance it starts from: look for the word “Jukes-Cantor” near the top.)

text:
Bonus: a rigorous tree, for real (IQ-TREE)






TipOptional, for students who are ahead



This is not part of the course. No marks depend on it, and no later session assumes you have done it. It exists because the theory block named two things FastTree approximates for speed, a proper substitution model and real bootstrap support, and leaves them “out of scope.” This bonus is that scope, on the exact same alignment you already have.


FastTree assumed a simple substitution model (Jukes-Cantor: every base equally likely to mutate into every other) and estimates support with a fast approximation (SH-like, roughly “how often does this split survive small random tweaks”). IQ-TREE does both properly, at real computational cost: ModelFinder tests dozens of substitution models (different rules for how often each base swaps for each other one, whether some sites mutate faster than others) and picks the one that fits your data best by a statistical criterion, then ultrafast bootstrap rebuilds the tree 1,000 times, each time from a random resample of the alignment’s columns, and reports what fraction of those 1,000 trees agree with each split in the final one. That is what a bootstrap support value (typically written as a percentage, out of 100) actually counts.

3.6.1 Try it (1-2 minutes to run)
module load IQ-TREE
iqtree3 -s aligned_spike.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T AUTO --prefix ../results/iqtree_bonus
-m MFP runs ModelFinder before building anything. -B 1000 requests 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. -T AUTO lets IQ-TREE pick how many threads to use.






NoteCheckpoint



This takes noticeably longer than FastTree, roughly a minute or two on LEGcompute, not under a second: proper model selection and 1,000 real resamples cost real time. When it finishes, ../results/iqtree_bonus.iqtree is a full text report; the one line to find is “Best-fit model according to BIC”. ../results/iqtree_bonus.treefile is the tree itself, in Newick format exactly like FastTree’s output, except each internal split is now labelled with a number out of 100 rather than FastTree’s 0-1 scale.


Open plot_tree.R, duplicate the line that reads the tree, and point the copy at "../results/iqtree_bonus.treefile" instead, to plot this one the same way. Two questions worth answering for yourself, not submitted anywhere:

Is the topology (which sequences group together) the same as your FastTree tree?
Are the bootstrap values close to FastTree’s support values, or different? Given that one is a fast approximation and the other resamples the data 1,000 times, what would you expect, and why might a real difference (if you see one) matter more on a harder dataset than on this one?



3.6.2 Go further
Open ../results/iqtree_bonus.iqtree in a text editor and find the “SUBSTITUTION PROCESS” section near the end, where “Rate parameter R” and “State frequencies” sit a few lines below the model name. These are the actual numbers ModelFinder fit to your data: for example, how much more often a transition (A<->G or C<->T) happens than a transversion, for these five coronavirus spike genes specifically, rather than assumed equal as FastTree’s default model assumes.

3.7 Answers






NoteOpen this after you have tried the exercises yourself





Session 3 has now been submitted. Below are the real answers, from the same commands run on LEGcompute: use them to check your own reasoning, not to replace it. Numbers that depend on live NCBI data (the total count, which 100 background genomes were fetched, the trimming percentages) change a little over time and between students: compare the pattern, not the last digit.
Who was unknown_sample? RaTG13 (MN996532.2), a coronavirus found in a horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus affinis) in China, and the closest known relative of SARS-CoV-2 (Zhou et al., Nature, 2020). Everything you found points to it: very close to SARS-CoV-2, but not one of them.
Section 1, setup. All six files present; the path ends in bioinfo_course/session_03/data.
Block B, quick search. One line:
unknown_sample  SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1  92.887  3824  256  5  1  3810  1  3822  0.0  5541
Block B, deep search. Four lines:
SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1   92.887  3824  ...  0.0       5671
SARS-CoV-1_Tor2         74.207  3718  ...  0.0       2345
MERS-CoV                75.472  106   ...  1.99e-13  68.0
HCoV-OC43_seasonal      85.714  42    ...  5.35e-08  50.0
MERS-CoV or HCoV-OC43, which is better supported? MERS-CoV. HCoV-OC43 has the higher pident (85.7% vs 75.5%), but on a match more than twice shorter (42 vs 106 bp); MERS-CoV has a much smaller evalue (1.99e-13 vs 5.35e-08) and a higher bitscore (68.0 vs 50.0). A high percent identity on a very short stretch means little: always read pident together with length, evalue and bitscore.
Block C, alignment window and whole-gene distances.

Do the two methods agree on MERS-CoV vs HCoV-OC43? No, this is the one real disagreement of the day: the whole-gene distance puts HCoV-OC43 (50.8%) marginally closer than MERS-CoV (51.3%), while the deep BLAST bitscore favours MERS-CoV. Both are about 50% different from unknown_sample: at that distance, small disagreements between methods are expected, and the honest conclusion is “both far, order uncertain”.
Block D, live NCBI fetch and tree.

NCBI holds millions of SARS-CoV-2 sequences (4,433,380 when tested; it keeps growing).
Your fetch: 114 sequences (100 background genomes, 13 named variants, unknown_sample).
MN908947.1 (Wuhan-Hu-1) was collected in China, in December 2019.
ClipKIT on the 114-sequence alignment: 326 of 30,937 sites trimmed (1.05%).
unknown_sample sits on its own long branch (about 0.07), 20 to 50 times longer than a typical branch between two SARS-CoV-2 genomes (0.0001 to 0.002).
The Omicron sublineages (BA.1 to 24C) form one connected group, apart from Alpha, Delta, Gamma and Mu.
Named variant closest to Wuhan-Hu-1: Delta, then Mu, Alpha and Gamma, before the Omicron sublineages branch off.
Rerooting on Wuhan-Hu-1: the groupings do not change (rerooting never changes who is related to whom), and the two plots look almost identical here, because Wuhan-Hu-1’s own branch is almost zero. unknown_sample is still the more defensible root: it really sits outside the group (long branch, and blocks B to D2), while Wuhan-Hu-1 is itself one of the 113 SARS-CoV-2 genomes.
Your background genomes are mostly very recent (2026 in our test fetch), much more recent than the named variants.

Your tree should look roughly like this one, drawn with the same plot_tree.R from the same pipeline run ahead of class. Yours may differ a little, because your 100 background genomes were not necessarily the same ones; what matters is the overall pattern:



The expected block D tree: unknown_sample alone on a very long branch, the named variants near the base in the order Wuhan-Hu-1, Delta, Mu, Alpha, Gamma, then the Omicron sublineages, and the 100 background genomes (unlabelled, in grey) further down.


Block D, continued (the 13 named variants only). ClipKIT trims 716 of 30,503 sites (2.35%), about twice the share trimmed from the 114-sequence alignment: with only 13 sequences, a few gappy columns weigh much more. In the EBI viewer, the Omicron columns look more similar to each other than to Wuhan_China’s, as the tree shows.
Block D2, protein vs nucleotide. SARS-CoV-2 vs SARS-CoV-1: 75.96% identity at the protein level, 74.21% at the nucleotide level. The protein is higher: several codons code for the same amino acid, so some DNA differences (synonymous substitutions) vanish at the protein level.
Section 5, your interpretation: a complete answer.

unknown_sample is most similar to SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1 at every level checked: 93% nucleotide identity over nearly the whole spike gene (both BLAST searches) and the smallest whole-gene distance in the alignment table (6.9%). SARS-CoV-1 is a clear second, both by BLAST (74.2% nucleotide, 76.0% protein identity) and by distance (25.7%). MERS-CoV and HCoV-OC43 are both far more distant, around 50% whole-gene difference, and the two methods do not fully agree on which of the two is further away. This pattern suggests that unknown_sample shares a recent common ancestor with SARS-CoV-2, closer than its relationship to SARS-CoV-1, and is only distantly related to the other two. In the 114-genome tree, it branches apart from all real SARS-CoV-2 genomes on a much longer branch, which confirms the same conclusion by a different method.

Good limitations: the conclusion rests on a single gene; a strict BLAST search alone would have missed three of the four references; MERS-CoV and HCoV-OC43 come out in a different order depending on the method.
Optional challenge A. Rooting on a background genome does not change which variants group together, but it makes the tree start inside the SARS-CoV-2 group itself: an arbitrary choice with no biological reason. unknown_sample is a real outgroup (long branch, and different by every measure), so the root it gives shows where the group actually starts.

NoteSources and reuse





The four named reference sequences are real NCBI RefSeq records, fetched directly for this course, both as nucleotide CDS and as protein: SARS-CoV-2 (NC_045512.2, protein YP_009724390.1), SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3, protein YP_009825051.1), MERS-CoV (NC_019843.3, protein YP_009047204.1), and HCoV-OC43 (NC_006213.1, protein YP_009555241.1). unknown_sample is a fifth real NCBI record, also a spike gene; its accession is kept out of this public page on purpose, since it is this session’s graded unknown. The alignment was built with MAFFT (--auto), precomputed so that the practical starts from a correct result. The SARS-CoV-2 protein accession (P0DTC2 in UniProt, YP_009724390.1 in NCBI) is the same record included in Session 1’s mystery.fasta. 4.1 Overview
Download the lecture slides (PDF)
Sessions 1-3 were about sequences: reading them, checking them, comparing them. From today, the course moves to tables: one row per sample, one column per measurement. This is the kind of data you will meet in almost every biology project, whatever the organism or the technique.
Today’s tables are real data from the lab: a soybean experiment where two cultivars grew under four climates. You will start very gently, with a clean R project and the plants themselves: where they stood in the experiment, what each one was used for, and how much the stresses weighed on them. You will then turn to the bacteria living on and around them (16S amplicon sequencing), reshape and summarise the tables with dplyr and tidyr, draw clearer plots with ggplot2, run your first statistical tests, from a t-test to a linear model that says which part of the climate actually matters, and write their results on your plots.

4.2 Theory (≈45 min)

4.2.1 1. A clean R project
An analysis is not just a result: it is something another person (or you, in six months) must be able to rerun. The simplest habit that makes this possible is one folder per analysis, always organised the same way:
session_04/
├── session_04.Rproj      <- double-click to open the project in RStudio
├── WORKBOOK.qmd          <- your report: code + plots + text, in one file
├── data/                 <- raw data: read it, never edit it by hand
│   ├── soybean_plants.csv
│   └── soybean_alpha_diversity.csv
├── img/                  <- images you did not make with R (photos, schemes)
│   └── experimental_design.png
└── results/              <- everything your code produces (figures, tables)
Three rules come with it:

Raw data is read-only. You never open the CSV in Excel to “fix” something: every change happens in code, so it is visible and repeatable.
Paths are relative. Inside the project, data/soybean_alpha_diversity.csv always works, on any computer. A path like C:/Users/me/Desktop/... only works on yours.
The report is the analysis. A Quarto file (.qmd) mixes text and code chunks. When you Render it, R runs every chunk from top to bottom, in a clean session. If it renders, it is reproducible.



4.2.2 2. Tidy tables and the grammar of graphics
A tidy table has one row per observation (here: one sample) and one column per variable (compartment, water, heat, shannon, …). Almost every tool in R expects this shape.
The tidyverse is a family of packages built around tidy tables (each one is described in the R toolbox below). You will use three of them today:

dplyr manipulates a table: keep some rows (filter), add or change a column (mutate), summarise by group (group_by + summarise);
tidyr reshapes a table: pivot_longer stacks several columns into one;
ggplot2 draws it. A ggplot is built in layers, joined with +:

ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ..., colour = ...)) +  # which table, which columns where
  geom_boxplot() +                                   # how to draw them
  facet_wrap(~ ...)                                  # one panel per group
Steps are chained with the pipe %>%, read as “and then”: take the table, and then keep the rhizoplane, and then compute the mean per group. It comes with the tidyverse, and RStudio types it for you with Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M.


4.2.3 3. From a boxplot to a linear model
A boxplot shows that two groups look different. A statistical test answers whether that difference is larger than the noise between plants, and a linear model also says how large it is.
The key idea for this course: most common tests are the same linear model. A t-test comparing watered and drought plants is lm(shannon ~ water). Add a second factor and it becomes a two-way ANOVA: lm(shannon ~ water * heat). The * means “each factor, and their interaction”: does the effect of drought depend on the heatwave?
anova(model) then splits the total variation into one piece per factor, plus the residuals (what no factor explains: plant-to-plant noise). Two numbers matter for each factor:

the p-value: could a difference this large appear by chance alone?
the share of variation it explains (its sum of squares divided by the total): how much does it actually matter?

They are not the same thing. With very little noise, a tiny difference can be highly significant. Always look at both, and at the plot.
Which test, when? Keep this table at hand for the rest of the course. Each test assumes something about the data; when the assumption clearly fails, use the alternative in the last column.

How to check the assumptions of a model: look at its residuals with plot(model, which = 1) (spread) and plot(model, which = 2) (normality). Formal tests exist (shapiro.test(residuals(model))), but the plots tell you more.


4.2.4 4. Worked example: the soybean experiment






Figure 4.1: The experiment: two soybean cultivars, four climates, and many kinds of measurements on the same plants (C. Maslard, PhD thesis).




2 cultivars, Stocata and Wendy, chosen for their contrasted root systems;
4 climates: a factorial design of water (watered, or drought: watering slowly withdrawn from 20% to 10% soil water content) × temperature (normal, or heatwave: two waves at 40 °C for three days);
plants grew in rhizotubes: flat, transparent pots holding two plants of the same condition, set out in lines and positions (you will draw this map in block B);
at the final harvest, each plant had one job, because most measurements destroy the plant:








analysis in your table
What was done with this plant

plant_microbiome
the bacteria on and inside the plant: rhizoplane, root endosphere, phylloplane



Two consequences you will meet today:

the biomass and the bacteria were measured on different plants of the same conditions: you can compare conditions, but not link one plant’s biomass to its own bacteria;
for the bacteria, each sample was sequenced (16S) and three alpha-diversity indices computed: richness (how many different bacteria), evenness (how equally they share the space), and shannon (combines both; higher = more diverse).



4.2.5 Practical briefing
Today you work in pairs for blocks A-D, and alone for block E. Block B introduces the experiment through the plants: where they stood, what each one was used for, and how much the stresses weighed on them. Blocks C and D then turn to the bacteria and walk you through the full analysis on one compartment, the rhizoplane: a plot, then the statistics, then the statistics on the plot. In block E, you analyse the bulk soil on your own, with a different kind of figure: the reasoning is the same, the code and the answer are not. Your submission is the rendered workbook: your bulk soil figure, its statistics, and your interpretation are what is graded.

text:
4.3 Your R toolbox
Read this once now, and come back to it whenever a function surprises you. One tab per package: what it is for, the functions you use today, one example, and the mistake everyone makes at least once.

tidyversereadrdplyrtidyrggplot2broom


What it is. Not one package but a family of packages designed to work together, all built around tidy tables. library(tidyverse) loads the core ones in one line, including the four below (readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2) and the pipe %>%.
The pipe %>%. Passes what is on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. These two lines do exactly the same thing:
summarise(group_by(alpha, compartment), mean_shannon = mean(shannon))

alpha %>%
  group_by(compartment) %>%
  summarise(mean_shannon = mean(shannon))
The second one reads top to bottom, like a recipe. Shortcut in RStudio: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M.
Common mistake. Forgetting library(tidyverse) after restarting R: every tidyverse function then fails with could not find function. Rendering always starts from a fresh session, which is why library() lives in the first chunk of the workbook.
Go further. R for Data Science (free online book), and all the Posit cheat sheets.


What it is for. Reading rectangular text files (CSV, TSV) into R as a tibble, the tidyverse version of a table.



Function
What it does




read_csv("data/file.csv")
read a comma-separated file


read_tsv("data/file.tsv")
read a tab-separated file


write_csv(table, "results/file.csv")
save a table you computed



What to check. read_csv() guesses each column’s type and tells you what it found: chr (text) or dbl (number). Always glance at that message, or at glimpse(): a column of numbers read as chr means something in the file is not a number (a comma decimal, a “NA” typed as “n/a”, a unit in a cell…).
Common mistake. A path that only works on your computer ("C:/Users/me/Desktop/data.csv"). Inside an R project, always write the path from the project folder: "data/soybean_alpha_diversity.csv".
Cheat sheet. Data import with readr


What it is for. Manipulating a table: choosing rows, creating columns, summarising groups. Each function is a verb, takes a table first, and returns a new table.








Verb
What it does
Today




filter()
keep the rows that match a condition
filter(compartment == "Rhizoplane")


mutate()
add a column or change one
mutate(compartment = factor(...))


count()
count rows per group
count(alpha, compartment)


group_by() + summarise()
one summary row per group
group_by(water) %>% summarise(mean = mean(shannon))


is.na()
TRUE where a value is missing; !is.na() keeps what is there
filter(!is.na(biomass_total))


pull()
take one column out of a table, as a plain value
filter(term == "heat") %>% pull(p.value)


select(), arrange()
keep some columns; sort rows
not needed today, good to know



Example. Mean Shannon diversity per compartment and water regime, sorted:
alpha %>%
  group_by(compartment, water) %>%
  summarise(mean_shannon = mean(shannon)) %>%
  arrange(mean_shannon)
With two grouping columns, summarise() prints a message about “grouped output”: it is information, not an error.
Common mistakes.

= instead of == in filter(). = gives a value to an argument, == tests equality. dplyr spots it and suggests the fix.
Forgetting the quotes: filter(compartment == Rhizoplane) looks for a column called Rhizoplane. Values of text columns always go in quotes, column names never.
A mutate() that is not saved: alpha %>% mutate(...) only shows the result. To keep it, assign it: alpha <- alpha %>% mutate(...).

Cheat sheet. Data transformation with dplyr


What it is for. Changing the shape of a table without changing its content.

Wide: one row per plant, one column per measurement (biomass_leaf, biomass_stem, biomass_root). Easy to read for a human, and the shape of plants.
Long: one row per plant and organ, with a column saying which organ it is (organ) and one with its value (biomass). The shape ggplot needs to put the organs side by side, or in their own panels.








Function
What it does




pivot_longer(cols, names_to, values_to)
wide → long: stack several columns into two


pivot_longer(..., names_prefix = "biomass_")
the same, removing the start of the old column names


pivot_wider(names_from, values_from)
long → wide: the exact reverse



organs <- physio %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(biomass_leaf, biomass_stem, biomass_root),
               names_to = "organ", names_prefix = "biomass_",
               values_to = "biomass")

organs %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = organ, values_from = biomass)   # back to one row per plant
The same works for the three diversity indices of alpha (richness, shannon, evenness).
How to think about it. Ask “what should one row be?”. For one box per organ, one row must be one organ of one plant, so: long.
Common mistake. Forgetting the quotes in names_to = "organ": the new column does not exist yet, so its name is text.
Cheat sheet. Data tidying with tidyr


What it is for. Plots, built layer by layer. Every ggplot has the same three parts:

data: which table (ggplot(alpha, ...));
aesthetics, inside aes(): which column goes where (x, y, colour, fill);
geometries, geom_...(): how to draw it (boxes, points, bars).

Then optional layers: facet_wrap() (one panel per group), labs() (titles and axis names), theme_bw() and friends (overall look).







Layer
Today




geom_boxplot()
distribution per group


geom_jitter(), geom_point()
one point per sample


geom_tile()
one rectangle per row, placed by x and y (a map)


geom_col()
bars whose height is a value (the share of variation)


geom_line()
lines joining points of the same group (interaction plot)


geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ..., ymax = ...))
error bars around a mean


facet_wrap(~ genotype)
one panel per cultivar


labs(x = ..., y = ..., subtitle = ...)
readable axis names, and a subtitle for your statistics


theme_bw()
a clean white background


ggsave("results/plot.png")
save the last plot



Example. The B3 plot, with readable labels and a cleaner theme:
ggplot(alpha, aes(x = compartment, y = shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = water), width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Shannon diversity", colour = "Water regime") +
  theme_bw()
Common mistakes.

%>% between layers instead of +. The pipe passes data; + adds layers. ggplot2 even asks “Did you use %>% instead of +?”.
A fixed colour inside aes(): aes(colour = "red") does not make points red, it creates a fake group called “red” (drawn in the default pink, with a legend). A fixed colour goes outside: geom_point(colour = "red"). Rule: inside aes() = a column, outside = a fixed value.

Cheat sheet. Data visualization with ggplot2


What it is for. Turning the output of a statistical model into a normal tibble, so you can filter it, compute with it, or plot it with ggplot, like any other table.







Function
What it returns




tidy(model)
one row per term: estimate, p-value…


tidy(anova(model))
the ANOVA table as a tibble (sumsq, p.value…)


glance(model)
one row for the whole model: R², number of observations…



Example: a t-test is a linear model. On the rhizoplane, with water as the only factor:
library(broom)
tidy(lm(shannon ~ water, data = rhizoplane))
The (Intercept) row is the mean Shannon diversity of the drought plants (the reference group, first in alphabetical order); the waterwatered row is how much higher the watered plants are, with its p-value. That is exactly what a t-test reports.
Common mistake. broom is installed with the tidyverse but not loaded by library(tidyverse): you need library(broom) once.
Documentation. broom.tidymodels.org

text:
4.4 Practical (≈1 h 50)

4.4.1 New R functions for today
This is the first R-heavy session, so the usual limit of four new functions does not hold: think of it as five ideas (read, reshape, plot, summarise, model), each with a few words of vocabulary.








Idea
Functions
Example




Read and look
library, read_csv, glimpse
alpha <- read_csv("data/soybean_alpha_diversity.csv")


Manipulate (dplyr)
filter, is.na, mutate, count, group_by + summarise
alpha %>% filter(compartment == "Rhizoplane")


Reshape (tidyr)
pivot_longer
pivot_longer(cols = c(biomass_leaf, biomass_root), names_to = "organ")


Plot (ggplot2)
ggplot, aes, geom_tile, geom_boxplot, geom_jitter, geom_point, geom_line, geom_errorbar, facet_wrap, labs, ggsave
ggplot(alpha, aes(x = compartment, y = shannon)) + geom_boxplot()


Test and model
t.test, TukeyHSD, aov, lm, anova, tidy, pull
anova(lm(shannon ~ water * heat, data = rhizoplane))









TipTested on LEGcompute



RStudio Server’s R (4.6.1) already has the tidyverse, broom, rmarkdown, and knitr installed, and RStudio Server ships its own Quarto: nothing to install, no module load needed today.




4.4.2 A. Build the R project, render once (15:00-15:15)
Open RStudio Server, then the Terminal tab (next to Console). You know these commands from Sessions 1-3:
mkdir -p ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/data ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/img ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/results
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_04/soybean_plants.csv ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/data/
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_04/soybean_alpha_diversity.csv ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/data/
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_04/experimental_design.png ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/img/
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_04/WORKBOOK.qmd ~/bioinfo_course/session_04/
ls -R ~/bioinfo_course/session_04
Now turn the folder into an R project: File → New Project → Existing Directory → Browse, pick ~/bioinfo_course/session_04, then Create Project. RStudio restarts inside the project: the Files pane now shows session_04.Rproj, WORKBOOK.qmd, data/, img/ and results/.
Open WORKBOOK.qmd, write your name at the top, and click Render (the blue arrow above the editor).






NoteCheckpoint



WORKBOOK.html appears next to WORKBOOK.qmd and opens in a new tab or the Viewer. It shows a few error messages from section B4 on: that is expected, those chunks still contain ___ blanks. Section A must show the glimpse() output without error.








Tip“Error: unexpected input”?



That is what R says when it meets a ___ you have not filled in yet. RStudio also marks the line with a red cross in the margin. Replace the ___ and run the chunk again.


From now on, run chunks one by one with the green ▶ button at the top right of each chunk (or Ctrl/Cmd + Enter for one line), and render again whenever you want to check the full report.
The first chunk of the workbook loads the packages and reads the plant table:
library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2 and the pipe
library(broom)       # turns statistical results into tables (used from D2 on)
plants <- read_csv("data/soybean_plants.csv")
glimpse(plants)
All library() calls go at the very top of a report: anyone reading it sees at once what it needs, and a later chunk that fails cannot take a package down with it.
glimpse() lists every column with its type: <chr> is text, <dbl> is a number. NA means “not available”: nothing was measured there.
Just below that chunk, the workbook shows the design of the experiment as Figure 1. It is not made by R: it is an image file, inserted with one line of text.






TipInsert an image into a Quarto report



One line, outside any code chunk:
![The soybean experiment (C. Maslard, PhD thesis).](img/experimental_design.png){#fig-design width=100%}

![...]: the caption, printed under the image as “Figure 1: …”;
(...): the path to the file, from the project folder, like read_csv();
{#fig-design width=100%}: a label, which must start with fig-, and options such as the width;
anywhere in your text, @fig-design becomes “Figure 1”, a link to the figure. Add a figure above it, and the numbers update themselves.

The rendered HTML still stays one single file: the image is packed inside it. You will do it yourself in block E, with the figure you save.








NoteCheckpoint



Rows: 240, Columns: 12. One row per plant of the final harvest: its rhizotube, its place (line, position), its condition (genotype, water, heat), its job (analysis) and, for some plants only, its dry biomass in grams (biomass_leaf, biomass_stem, biomass_root, biomass_total).




4.4.3 B. Meet the experiment: the plants (15:15-15:50)
Before looking at any bacteria, understand the experiment they come from, and check that the stresses really hurt the plants.
B1. Who did what? Count the plants per job, then per condition:
count(plants, analysis)
count(plants, heat, water, genotype)






NoteCheckpoint



Four jobs: 66 physiology, 53 exudates, 75 omics_and_soil, 46 plant_microbiome. Eight conditions, 26 to 34 plants each: the design is not perfectly balanced, because some plants died or were replaced during the experiment.


B2. The map of the experiment. Each rhizotube had a line and a position. Draw them as a map: one tile per rhizotube, coloured by water regime, with a symbol for the cultivar, and one map per heat regime:
ggplot(plants, aes(x = position, y = line)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = water), colour = "white") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = genotype)) +
  facet_wrap(~ heat, ncol = 1)
geom_tile() draws one rectangle per row of the table (the two plants of a rhizotube fall on the same tile); fill colours the inside of a shape, shape changes the symbol of a point.








Figure 4.2: Checkpoint B2: the map of the experiment, one tile per rhizotube.





Look at it before you go on. Are the watered and drought rhizotubes grouped together, or mixed? Why would an experimenter mix them on purpose? Compare the two maps. The empty cells held plants harvested earlier, for another part of the experiment.
B3. Did the stresses hurt the plants? Only the physiology and exudates plants were weighed: for the others, the biomass columns are NA. Keep the plants that have a biomass, then plot it:
physio <- plants %>%
  filter(!is.na(biomass_total))

ggplot(physio, aes(x = water, y = biomass_total, colour = heat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ genotype)
is.na(biomass_total) is TRUE when the biomass is missing; the ! in front means “not”. So filter(!is.na(biomass_total)) keeps the plants that were weighed.
B4. The same thing as numbers.
physio %>%
  group_by(water, heat) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_biomass = mean(biomass_total))






NoteCheckpoint



physio has 108 plants. Mean dry biomass: about 1.25 g (watered, normal), 1.16 g (watered, heatwave), 0.50 g (drought, normal), 0.32 g (drought, heatwave). Drought divides the plant’s biomass by more than two; the heatwave takes a little more on top.


B5. Which organ suffers most? (tidyr) The biomass of each organ sits in its own column. To draw the three organs side by side, ggplot needs them stacked in one column, with a second column saying which organ each value belongs to. That is what pivot_longer does:
organs <- physio %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(biomass_leaf, biomass_stem, biomass_root),
               names_to = "organ",
               names_prefix = "biomass_",
               values_to = "biomass")

ggplot(organs, aes(x = organ, y = biomass, fill = water)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ heat)
names_prefix = "biomass_" removes the start of the column names, so the organs are simply called leaf, stem and root. organs has three times more rows than physio: one per plant and organ.






NoteCheckpoint



organs has 324 rows (108 × 3). Under drought, every organ loses roughly two thirds of its biomass, but not exactly the same share: compare the root with the leaf.




4.4.4 15:50-16:00: Checkpoint and short break
Before the break: the map and the biomass plots drawn, and the B questions of the workbook answered. Click Render once to check that sections A and B now render without red errors.


4.4.5 C. The bacteria: first look, then the rhizoplane (16:00-16:15, pairs)
The plants are clearly stressed. Do their bacteria feel it?
C1. A second table. Read the bacterial diversity table and count the samples per compartment:
alpha <- read_csv("data/soybean_alpha_diversity.csv")
count(alpha, compartment)






NoteCheckpoint



195 samples. Each compartment was sampled on 40 plants (5 per condition), but some compartments have fewer than 40 samples: a few failed (too little DNA, too few reads) and were removed before you got the table.


C2. Diversity from the soil to the leaf. The compartments come out in alphabetical order by default, which makes no biological sense. Fix the order with mutate(), then plot every sample:
alpha <- alpha %>%
  mutate(compartment = factor(compartment,
                              levels = c("Bulk soil", "Rhizosphere", "Rhizoplane",
                                         "Root endosphere", "Phylloplane")))

ggplot(alpha, aes(x = compartment, y = shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = water), width = 0.2)








Figure 4.3: Checkpoint C2: Shannon diversity per compartment, one point per sample.





Which compartments differ from which? With five groups, that is a job for an ANOVA followed by a Tukey test (see the table in the theory part), in one line:
TukeyHSD(aov(shannon ~ compartment, data = alpha))
One row per pair of compartments: diff is the difference of their means, p adj its p-value, corrected for the fact that you test ten pairs at once.






NoteCheckpoint



Bulk soil vs rhizosphere: p adj close to 1 (no difference). Rhizoplane vs phylloplane: 0.12. Every other pair: below 0.01. The spread is very different between compartments (look at the plot), which an ANOVA does not like: the table’s alternative, kruskal.test(shannon ~ compartment, data = alpha), reaches the same conclusion.


C3. Keep one compartment. Comparing climates across compartments would mix two very different questions. Work on one compartment at a time, starting with the rhizoplane:
rhizoplane <- alpha %>%
  filter(compartment == "Rhizoplane")

count(rhizoplane, water, heat, genotype)






NoteCheckpoint



39 samples, 8 combinations of water × heat × genotype, 4 or 5 samples each.


C4. Plot the design. The same kind of plot as for the biomass in B3:
ggplot(rhizoplane, aes(x = water, y = shannon, colour = heat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ genotype)








Figure 4.4: Checkpoint C4: rhizoplane Shannon diversity by water, heat and cultivar.





Before any statistics: which of the three factors seems to change Shannon diversity the most? Is it the same factor that weighed most on the plant’s biomass in B3? Write your guess in the workbook.


4.4.6 D. Guided: the statistics (16:15-16:35, pairs)
D1. Two groups: a t-test. Start with the simplest question: do watered and drought plants differ?
rhizoplane %>%
  group_by(water) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_shannon = mean(shannon))

t.test(shannon ~ water, data = rhizoplane, var.equal = TRUE)
Read ~ as “explained by”: Shannon explained by water. var.equal = TRUE asks for the classic t-test, the one that assumes both groups vary as much.






NoteCheckpoint



Means of 2.40 (drought) and 3.24 (watered); the t-test gives p-value = 2.601e-06.


D2. The same test, as a linear model. Now fit lm() with the same formula, and read it with tidy() from the broom package (loaded in section A):
tidy(lm(shannon ~ water, data = rhizoplane))
Two rows. (Intercept) is the mean of the drought plants (the reference group: first in alphabetical order). waterwatered is how much higher the watered plants are, and its p.value is exactly the t-test’s p-value. A t-test is a linear model with one factor: this is why the next step can simply add more factors.
D3. All three factors at once. One line fits water, heat, genotype and all their interactions; one more line splits the variation:
model_rhizoplane <- lm(shannon ~ water * heat * genotype, data = rhizoplane)
anova(model_rhizoplane)
Read the table row by row: one row per factor or interaction, Residuals last. The column Pr(>F) is the p-value; R adds stars to the small ones.






NoteCheckpoint



Only one row has three stars: water, with Pr(>F) = 4.01e-06. heat is close (0.06) but above 0.05. No interaction is significant.


D4. How much does each factor explain? The p-value says whether; the share of variation says how much. tidy() also turns the ANOVA table into a normal tibble, so you can compute with it:
anova_rhizoplane <- tidy(anova(model_rhizoplane)) %>%
  mutate(share = sumsq / sum(sumsq))
anova_rhizoplane

ggplot(anova_rhizoplane, aes(x = "Rhizoplane", y = share, fill = term)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of variation in Shannon diversity")
One bar, cut into slices: the bigger the slice, the more that factor explains. The Residuals slice is everything the design does not explain.






NoteCheckpoint



water explains about 45% of the variation, the residuals about 45%, and everything else together about 10%.


D5. Put the statistics on the plot. A figure should carry its own evidence. Keep the p-value in an object, then write it in the plot’s subtitle with paste(), which glues pieces of text together:
p_water <- t.test(shannon ~ water, data = rhizoplane, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
p_water

ggplot(rhizoplane, aes(x = water, y = shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Rhizoplane",
       subtitle = paste("t-test, drought vs watered: p =", signif(p_water, 2)),
       x = NULL, y = "Shannon diversity") +
  theme_bw()
$p.value takes one element out of the test result. signif(p_water, 2) keeps two significant digits, so the subtitle reads p = 2.6e-06 instead of fifteen digits.








Figure 4.5: Checkpoint D5: the t-test p-value written on the plot.







4.4.7 E. Alone: the bulk soil (16:35-16:55)
Now the bulk soil, the soil in the pot that does not touch the root. This time you do not redraw the same boxplot: you build a different kind of figure, an interaction plot, and put the statistics on it. Section E of the workbook guides you with a skeleton and a few ___ to fill.
What an interaction plot shows. One point per group mean, with an error bar (here the standard error: how precisely the mean is known), and a line joining the means of the same heat regime across the two water regimes. How to read it:

a line that goes up or down: the water regime changes Shannon diversity;
two lines far apart: the heat regime changes Shannon diversity;
two lines that are not parallel: an interaction, the effect of drought depends on the heatwave.

You need three new geometries, all in the ggplot2 tab of the toolbox: geom_point() for the means, geom_line() to join them (with group = heat in aes(), so ggplot knows which points to join), and geom_errorbar() for the bars. The means and standard errors come from a group_by() + summarise(), as in B4.
Then, in the workbook:

E1. Keep the bulk soil samples and count them (adapt C3).
E2. Compute the means and standard errors, and draw the interaction plot.
E3. Fit the three-factor model and compute the share of variation (adapt D3-D4).
E4. Write the ANOVA p-values of heat and water on your plot (adapt D5), give it readable labels, and save it with ggsave():

ggsave("results/bulk_soil_interaction.png", width = 6, height = 4)
ggsave() saves the last plot drawn into results/. Then insert that file into your report yourself, below the chunk, as in the callout of block A: a caption of your own that says what the figure shows, the label #fig-bulk, a width of 80%. Cite it as @fig-bulk in your answer to E5. Then answer the E questions: they are the graded part of today. Compare with the rhizoplane: is the answer the same? Is the most significant effect also a large one, in Shannon units? Look at the y axis of your plot before you answer.


4.4.8 Wrap-up (16:55-17:00)
Click Render one last time. Check that WORKBOOK.html shows your bulk soil figure and your ANOVA table, and that results/bulk_soil_interaction.png exists. You can finish the written answers at home: submit WORKBOOK.html on Moodle by Sunday evening (18 October). Your workbook file still says “Thursday” at the top: the date on this page is the right one.
If your workbook refuses to render at the end, do not panic: submit WORKBOOK.qmd instead, and say in the last section where it fails.

4.6 Optional challenge
For your own interest, not graded.
A. All five compartments in one figure. Repeat D3-D4 for the rhizosphere, the root endosphere and the phylloplane, add a compartment column to each anova_... table with mutate(), stack them with bind_rows(), and draw one bar per compartment with geom_col(). Is there a pattern from soil to leaf?
B. Check the model’s assumptions. A linear model assumes the residuals are roughly normal and equally spread across groups. plot(model_rhizoplane, which = 1) and plot(model_rhizoplane, which = 2) draw the two classic diagnostic plots. Do the rhizoplane residuals look acceptable?
C. The plant is not independent. The rhizoplane and the root endosphere come from the same plants (look at the plant column). Fitting one model on both compartments at once, with the plant as a random effect, is what a mixed model does: lme4::lmer(shannon ~ compartment * water + (1 | plant), data = ...). What changes compared to two separate models?
D. Does the place in the experiment matter? Colour the map by biomass instead of water regime, with one panel per climate so that the drought effect does not hide everything else:
ggplot(physio, aes(x = position, y = line, fill = biomass_total)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_grid(heat ~ water)
Do the plants at one end of the lines, or on one line, look bigger? Then test it: add + line + position at the end of a model of biomass_total. Why does the mixing you saw in B2 protect the conclusions even if position has a small effect?
E. Two stresses together. Fit lm(biomass_total ~ water * heat * genotype, data = physio), look at its ANOVA table, then fit the same model on log(biomass_total). The interaction water:heat changes a lot. Compute, from B4, by how many percent the heatwave reduces the biomass of watered plants, and of drought plants. What does the log scale see that the raw scale missed, and what does it mean for a plant facing both stresses at once?

4.9 Answers






NoteOpen this after you have tried the exercises yourself





Session 4 has now been submitted. Below are the real answers, computed with the exact workbook code on LEGcompute: use them to check your own reasoning, not to replace it. Small rounding differences (second decimal) are normal.
A1. The plant table. 240 rows, 12 columns. One row is one plant of the final harvest. NA in the biomass columns: the plant was not weighed, because it was used for another job (omics and soil, plant microbiome), or the measure failed.
B1. Plants per job. 66 physiology, 53 exudates, 75 omics_and_soil, 46 plant_microbiome. The rhizoplane bacteria come from the plant_microbiome plants; the bulk soil bacteria from the soil of the omics_and_soil plants.
B2. The map. The conditions are mixed: watered and drought rhizotubes, and the two cultivars, alternate along the lines. Mixing on purpose (randomisation) prevents a place effect (light, draught, the edge of the bench) from being mistaken for a treatment effect. The two maps have exactly the same layout: the same randomisation plan was used for both heat regimes.
B4. Biomass per climate. 108 plants weighed.

B5. Per organ. 324 rows = 108 plants × 3 organs. Mean biomass, watered → drought: leaf 0.61 → 0.19 g (−68%), stem 0.39 → 0.13 g (−66%), root 0.21 → 0.08 g (−61%). The root keeps the largest share of its biomass (its share of the total rises from 18% to 20%): keeping roots helps the plant explore the soil for the little water left.
C1. The bacteria table. Rhizoplane (39), rhizosphere (39) and root endosphere (37) have fewer than 40 samples: 5 compartments × 40 plants = 200 expected, 195 present, 5 missing.

Most diverse: rhizosphere and bulk soil (about 5). Least: root endosphere (about 2.2). Tukey: only two pairs do not differ, Rhizosphere-Bulk soil (p adj = 0.9988) and Phylloplane-Rhizoplane (0.1206); Root endosphere-Rhizoplane 0.0072, all the others below 0.0001. Why fewer bacteria inside the root: the root is a filter. Few soil bacteria can cross the root surface and live inside the tissues; the plant’s immune system and the chemistry inside the root select a small, specialised community.
C3. The rhizoplane. 39 samples, 8 combinations, 5 each except drought × normal × Stocata (4).
C4. Your guess. Water, the factor that weighed most on biomass: checked in D4.
D1. t-test. Watered 3.24, drought 2.40 (a drop of 0.84 Shannon units). t = −5.54, df = 37, p-value = 2.601e-06.
D2. The same test as a linear model. (Intercept) 2.40 is the drought mean; waterwatered 0.839 is the difference between the two means (3.24 − 2.40). Its p-value, 2.60e-06, is identical to the t-test’s: a t-test is a linear model with one factor.
D3. Three factors at once. Only water is below 0.05: Pr(>F) = 4.01e-06. heat 0.060, genotype 0.43, no interaction below 0.2. (If you changed the order of the factors in the formula, heat can come out at 0.046: with this design, the order matters a little.)
D4. Share of variation. Water 45.4%, residuals 45.1%, heat 5.5%, water:heat 2.4%, everything else below 1% each. Your C4 guess (water) was right.
D5. The p-value on the plot. t-test, drought vs watered: p = 2.6e-06. Computed in R, not typed: no typing error, and it updates by itself if the data or the test change.
E. The bulk soil, the code. One way to write it:
# E1
bulk_soil <- alpha %>%
  filter(compartment == "Bulk soil")
count(bulk_soil, water, heat, genotype)

# E2
bulk_soil_means <- bulk_soil %>%
  group_by(water, heat) %>%
  summarise(mean_shannon = mean(shannon),
            se = sd(shannon) / sqrt(n()))

plot_bulk_soil <- ggplot(bulk_soil_means,
                         aes(x = water, y = mean_shannon, colour = heat, group = heat)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_shannon - se, ymax = mean_shannon + se), width = 0.1)

# E3
model_bulk_soil <- lm(shannon ~ water * heat * genotype, data = bulk_soil)
anova_bulk_soil <- tidy(anova(model_bulk_soil)) %>%
  mutate(share = sumsq / sum(sumsq))

# E4
p_heat  <- anova_bulk_soil %>% filter(term == "heat") %>% pull(p.value)
p_water <- anova_bulk_soil %>% filter(term == "water") %>% pull(p.value)

plot_bulk_soil +
  labs(title = "Bulk soil",
       subtitle = paste("ANOVA: heat p =", signif(p_heat, 2),
                        "| water p =", signif(p_water, 2)),
       x = "Water regime", y = "Mean Shannon diversity (± SE)", colour = "Heat regime") +
  theme_bw()

ggsave("results/bulk_soil_interaction.png", width = 6, height = 4)
Then, below the chunk, the image line:
![Bulk soil: mean Shannon diversity (± SE) under the four climates. The heatwave lowers it slightly; drought does not.](results/bulk_soil_interaction.png){#fig-bulk width=80%}
E1. 40 samples, 5 per combination (fully balanced).
E2. Means: drought × heatwave 4.91, drought × normal 5.05, watered × heatwave 4.97, watered × normal 5.06 (SE about 0.02). Heat moves the means the most: the two lines are far apart, while each line is almost flat from drought to watered. The lines are roughly parallel: no clear interaction. Non-parallel lines would mean that the effect of drought depends on the heat regime.
E3. Only heat is significant: Pr(>F) = 1.45e-05, 42.0% of the variation. Water 3.2% (p = 0.17), genotype 1.1%, no significant interaction (water:heat p = 0.35), residuals 51.5%. The heatwave lowers diversity by about 0.1 Shannon units, against 0.84 for drought on the rhizoplane: about eight times smaller.
E4. Your figure should look like this one, and appear as Figure 2:



The expected E4 figure: the bulk soil interaction plot, four means with their standard errors, one line per heat regime.


Look at the y axis: it runs from about 4.90 to 5.07. ggplot zooms in, so a difference of 0.1 looks as large as the 0.84 of the rhizoplane.
E5. A complete answer.

In the bulk soil, drought does not change bacterial diversity (p = 0.17, 3% of the variation), whereas the heatwave lowers it slightly (from about 5.05 to 4.94, p = 1.5e-05, 42% of the variation; Figure 2). On the rhizoplane it is the opposite: drought is the main factor (3.24 to 2.40, p = 4e-06, 45% of the variation) and the heatwave is not significant. Drought probably acts through the plant: a thirsty root changes what it releases and how much water it draws right at its surface, while the soil further away hardly feels it. The bulk soil heatwave effect is highly significant but tiny (about 0.1 Shannon units, against 0.84 for drought on the rhizoplane): bulk soil samples vary so little that even a small difference stands out.

The key idea: significant is not large. A very small p-value says the difference is unlikely to be chance, not that it matters biologically.
E6. Good limitations. The bulk soil effect is significant but very small, and the zoomed y axis makes it look large; only 5 plants per combination; Shannon is one number and says nothing about which bacteria changed; biomass and bacteria come from different plants, so no plant-by-plant link is possible; one experiment, one season; the model’s assumptions were not checked; several compartments and many tests, so some p-values below 0.05 can appear by chance.

A pattern from soil to leaf: drought matters more and more as you come closer to the root surface (bulk soil 3%, rhizosphere 15%, rhizoplane 45%), but not inside the root, where the plant filters its bacteria. The heatwave matters where the bacteria are exposed to the air temperature: the bulk soil and the leaf surface.
Optional challenge B. The rhizoplane residuals look acceptable: no clear trend or funnel on the first plot, points close to the line on the second (Shapiro test p = 0.25), and a similar spread in both water regimes (sd 0.48 under drought, 0.46 watered).
Optional challenge C. 36 of the 40 plants have both a rhizoplane and an endosphere sample. In the mixed model, the plant effect has a standard deviation of 0.42, against 0.66 for the residuals: about 28% of the remaining variation is shared by the two compartments of the same plant. Two separate models treat these samples as independent, which they are not. The conclusion does not change: drought lowers the rhizoplane (+0.83 when watered) but hardly the endosphere (the compartment:water interaction, −0.70, cancels most of it: t = −2.28).

Even if position had a small effect, the mixing protects the conclusions: any place effect is spread over all conditions instead of piling up on one.

From B4, the heatwave removes about 7% of a watered plant’s biomass (1.25 → 1.16 g) but 35% of a drought plant’s (0.50 → 0.32 g). A log scale compares ratios, not differences: in relative terms, the two stresses together hurt more than the sum of each alone. That is how a plant biologist usually thinks about growth.

title: 5  Session 5: Many variables at once: PCA, heatmaps and PLS-DA
text:
5.2 Theory (≈45 min)

5.2.1 1. From one variable to many
Each sample now has one value per metabolite. For the analyses of today, the table must have one row per sample and one column per metabolite: a matrix. Your data file is long (one row per sample and metabolite, as in Session 4), so the first step is pivot_wider(), the reverse of the pivot_longer() you used in Session 4.
Two more steps before any multivariate method:

log-transform: concentrations go from 0.02 to about 190,000. On the raw scale, a few very abundant molecules would dominate everything. log10() turns ratios into differences: a molecule that doubles moves by the same amount, whether it is rare or abundant.
scale: each metabolite is centred and divided by its standard deviation, so that each one has the same weight in the analysis (scale. = TRUE in prcomp()).



5.2.2 2. Unsupervised: PCA and clustering
A PCA (principal component analysis) summarises the 34 columns into a few new axes, the principal components. PC1 is the direction along which the samples differ the most, PC2 the next one, at right angles, and so on. Three things to read:

the share of variance of each axis: how much of the differences between samples it captures;
the scores: where each sample falls on the axes (the usual PCA plot);
the loadings: how much each metabolite contributes to each axis, and in which direction.

A heatmap with clustering shows the whole matrix as colours, and reorders rows and columns so that similar ones sit next to each other. The trees (dendrograms) show the groups found.
In the practical, you first run a PCA on data you know without any biology: 41 decathlon performances, 10 events each. You will see the axes rediscover the best athletes, and why scaling matters when the variables are in different units (seconds and metres).
Both are unsupervised: they never see your labels (water, heat). If the samples still group by condition, the condition is a major source of variation in the data.


5.2.3 3. Supervised: PLS-DA, and why it must be validated
A PLS-DA (partial least squares discriminant analysis) is told the groups, and looks for the combination of metabolites that best separates them. It is useful to find which molecules distinguish two conditions, but it is dangerous: with many variables and few samples, it can separate any groups, even groups drawn at random. A separation on the data the model learned from proves nothing.
The answer is cross-validation: hide part of the samples, train the model on the rest, predict the hidden samples, repeat. Only the accuracy on samples the model did not see tells you whether the separation is real. You will see this trap with your own eyes in block D.


5.2.4 4. Many tests at once: the volcano plot
You can also test each metabolite on its own: one t-test per molecule, as in Session 4. With 34 tests at the 5% level, you expect about 1 or 2 “significant” results by chance alone. Correcting the p-values (here with the Benjamini-Hochberg method, which controls the false discovery rate) keeps that under control.
A volcano plot shows all the tests at once: the effect on the x axis (log2 fold change: positive means higher under drought), the evidence on the y axis (−log10 of the adjusted p-value: the higher, the stronger).
Which method, when?









Your question

In R

PLS-DA, always with cross-validation

yes


Which variables change between two groups, one by one?

(it is a test)





5.2.5 5. Worked example: the metabolome of the soybean plants
Today’s data come from the plants you met in Session 4, measured with two kinds of metabolomics:









Targeted
Untargeted

Root, stem, leaf (targeted): the omics_and_soil plants, frozen at harvest and ground; 4 samples per cultivar and condition, each a pool of two plants.
Exudates (targeted and untargeted): what the roots of the exudates plants released into a solution, collected at harvest; one sample per plant.

The exudates are the molecules the root gives to the soil: the food and the signals of the bacteria you studied in Session 4.

The warm-up runs a first PCA on data you can check with common sense: decathlon athletes and their 10 events. Blocks C and D analyse the root, guided: first without labels (PCA, heatmap), then with labels (PLS-DA, volcano). In block E, you analyse the leaf: same reasoning, a different answer.
