5.3 Your R toolbox
New tools today, on top of the Session 4 toolbox (still valid: see the Session 4 R toolbox).

tidyr: long → widePCA (base R)pheatmapmixOmicsggrepel


pivot_wider() is the reverse of pivot_longer(): it spreads one column into many.
root_wide <- root_long %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = metabolite, values_from = log_conc)

names_from: the column whose values become the new column names (here: the metabolite names);
values_from: the column that fills the new columns (here: the log concentrations).

Then select(-sample, ...) and as.matrix() keep the numbers only, as a matrix, and rownames() puts the sample names back on the rows.
Common mistake. Keeping a column that differs inside a sample (such as the raw concentration next to log_conc): pivot_wider() then cannot put one sample on one row. Select only the columns you need before pivoting.


prcomp() is part of R itself: no package needed.







Code
What it gives




prcomp(matrix, scale. = TRUE)
the PCA, each variable scaled


summary(pca)$importance[2, ]
the share of variance of each axis


pca$x
the scores: one row per sample, one column per axis


pca$rotation
the loadings: one row per variable, one column per axis



Reading the loadings. A metabolite with a large negative loading on PC1 is high in the samples on the left of the PCA plot; a large positive loading, high on the right.
Common mistake. Forgetting scale. = TRUE: the variables with the largest numbers then decide everything.


pheatmap(t(root_matrix), scale = "row", annotation_col = annotation,
         show_colnames = FALSE, fontsize_row = 7)

t() turns the matrix around: metabolites in rows, samples in columns;
scale = "row": each metabolite is shown as “above or below its own average” (z-score), otherwise the most abundant ones would fill the colour scale;
annotation_col: a small table, one row per sample (with the sample names as row names), whose columns become coloured bars on top;
the trees on the left and on top are the clustering: they are computed from the data, not from the annotation.



The reference package for PLS-DA (and much more) in biology.







Code
What it does




plsda(matrix, groups, ncomp = 2)
fits a PLS-DA with 2 components


plotIndiv(model, ellipse = TRUE, legend = TRUE)
the sample plot, with one ellipse per group


predict(model, matrix)$class$max.dist
the predicted group of each sample


perf(model, validation = "Mfold", folds = 4, nrepeat = 10)
cross-validation: 4 folds, repeated 10 times


perf(...)$error.rate$BER
the balanced error rate, per component (accuracy = 1 − error)



Install once, load every time. BiocManager::install("mixOmics", update = FALSE) runs once, in the Console (block A0). library(mixOmics) goes at the top of every report. Never put an install line in your workbook: every Render would install it again.
Common mistake: load it first. mixOmics loads another package (MASS) that also has a function called select(). Whatever is loaded last wins. So load mixOmics before the tidyverse; otherwise select() stops working, with a confusing error (“unused argument”).
Documentation. mixomics.org


geom_text_repel() writes text labels on a plot and moves them so that they do not overlap, unlike geom_text().
geom_text_repel(data = slice_min(root_tests, p_adjusted, n = 10),
                aes(label = metabolite), size = 3)
data = ... labels only some of the points: here, the 10 with the smallest adjusted p-values (slice_min(), from dplyr).

text:
5.4 Practical (≈1 h 50)






TipTested on LEGcompute



pheatmap and ggrepel are already installed in RStudio Server’s R. mixOmics is not: each of you installs it once, at the start of block A, in about 1 to 2 minutes (tested: 83 seconds, mixOmics 6.36.0).



5.4.1 A. Install mixOmics, same habits, new data (15:00-15:15)
A0. Install mixOmics, once. In the Console (not in the workbook), run these three lines:
dir.create(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
.libPaths(c(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), .libPaths()))
BiocManager::install("mixOmics", update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)

line 1 creates your personal R library, a folder in your home where you can install packages (you cannot write in the shared one);
line 2 tells R to use it, from now on in this session;
line 3 installs mixOmics from Bioconductor (a repository of biology packages), with the few packages it still needs. update = FALSE is important: otherwise R offers to update dozens of packages you already have.

It takes 1 to 2 minutes, and prints a lot of compilation messages: that is normal. While it runs, go on with the Terminal commands below.






NoteCheckpoint



The Console ends with * DONE (mixOmics). Then library(mixOmics) in the Console loads it without error (a few welcome lines are printed). You will never need to install it again: from now on, R finds it in your personal library.


A1. The project. In the Terminal tab:

cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_05/soybean_metabolites.csv ~/bioinfo_course/session_05/data/
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_05/soybean_exudates_untargeted.csv ~/bioinfo_course/session_05/data/

cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_05/decathlon.csv ~/bioinfo_course/session_05/data/

Then File → New Project → Existing Directory, pick ~/bioinfo_course/session_05, open WORKBOOK.qmd, write your name at the top and click Render once.






NoteCheckpoint



WORKBOOK.pdf appears (RStudio opens it), with the design figure as Figure 1, and the first chunk lists the columns sample, organ, genotype, water, heat, panel, metabolite, kegg_id, concentration. A few chunks further down show Error: unexpected input: those are the ___ you will fill.


panel is the analytical panel that measured each compound (amino acids, organic acids, flavonoids, phytohormones, cytokinins), as in the lab’s files: a practical grouping, not always the strict chemical family. concentration was cleaned before class: values below the detection limit were replaced by half of the smallest value measured for that molecule, a common rule in metabolomics.


5.4.2 B. One molecule at a time (15:10-15:35)
B1. What is in the table?
# how many samples per organ? (count by the column that holds the organ)
metabolites %>% distinct(organ, sample) %>% count(___)
metabolites %>% distinct(organ, metabolite) %>% count(organ)






NoteCheckpoint



Two small tables, each with one row per organ: exudate, leaf, root, stem. If you see one row per sample instead, check what you put in count().


B2. The drought hormone. Abscisic acid (ABA) makes the leaves close their stomata, the small pores through which they lose water. Look at it in the three organs (it is not on the exudate list):
aba <- metabolites %>%
  filter(metabolite == "Abscisic Acid")

# one panel per organ
ggplot(aba, aes(x = water, y = concentration, colour = heat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ ___, scales = "free_y")

# the mean per organ and per water regime
aba %>%
  group_by(organ, ___) %>%
  summarise(mean_aba = mean(concentration))
scales = "free_y" gives each organ its own y axis: the levels are very different between organs.
B3. Proline, a small amino acid that protects cells when water is short. Same plot, with one ___ to fill.
B4. Why the log?
range(metabolites$___)

ggplot(metabolites, aes(x = concentration)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50)

# the same histogram, on the log10 scale
ggplot(metabolites, aes(x = log10(___))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50)






NoteCheckpoint



range() prints two numbers. The first histogram is one tall bar near zero; the second one is spread out and readable.




5.4.3 15:35-15:45: Short break


5.4.4 Warm-up: what a PCA does, on athletes (15:45-16:00, pairs)
Before 34 metabolites, a PCA on data you can check with common sense: 41 decathlon performances (Decastar meeting and Athens Olympic Games, 2004; data of the FactoMineR package). Each athlete did 10 events: four runs (times in seconds, small is good) and six jumps and throws (metres, large is good).
W1. The table.
decathlon <- read_csv("data/decathlon.csv")
glimpse(decathlon)

# how many athletes per competition?
decathlon %>% count(___)
W2. Without and with scaling. The same PCA twice: first with each event in its own unit, then with every event scaled.
# the 10 events only, as a matrix, with the athletes' names as row names
events <- decathlon %>%
  select(run_100m:run_1500m) %>%
  as.matrix()
rownames(events) <- decathlon$___

# how much does each event vary between athletes? (standard deviation, in its own unit)
decathlon %>% summarise(across(run_100m:run_1500m, sd))

# a PCA WITHOUT scaling: each event keeps its own unit (seconds, metres)
pca_raw <- prcomp(events, scale. = FALSE)
round(pca_raw$rotation[, 1], 2)   # the loadings on PC1

# the same PCA WITH scaling: every event gets the same weight
decathlon_pca <- prcomp(events, scale. = ___)
decathlon_variance <- round(100 * summary(decathlon_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
decathlon_variance
across(run_100m:run_1500m, sd) applies sd() to every column from run_100m to run_1500m.
W3. Arrows and points. The loadings become arrows (one per event), the scores points (one per athlete):
# the events: one arrow per event, from 0 to its loadings on PC1 and PC2
decathlon_loadings <- as_tibble(decathlon_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "event")

ggplot(decathlon_loadings) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = ___, yend = ___),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = ___)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", decathlon_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", decathlon_variance[2], "%)"))

# the athletes: one point per athlete, coloured by the final score
decathlon_scores <- as_tibble(decathlon_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(decathlon, athlete, competition, points))

ggplot(decathlon_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = athlete), size = 3) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", decathlon_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", decathlon_variance[___], "%)"))

# does PC1 follow the final score?
cor(decathlon_scores$PC1, decathlon_scores$___)






NoteCheckpoint



Two plots: one with 10 arrows (one per event), one with 41 points. Some names appear twice, because 9 athletes competed in both meetings. On another computer, the whole plot may be flipped left-right or up-down: the direction of an axis is arbitrary, only the angles between arrows matter.




5.4.5 C. Guided: the whole root metabolome, without labels (16:00-16:35, pairs)
C1. From long to wide. One row per sample, one column per metabolite, log10 of the concentration:
# one row per sample, one column per metabolite, log10 of the concentration
root_wide <- metabolites %>%
  filter(organ == ___) %>%
  mutate(log_conc = ___(concentration)) %>%
  select(sample, genotype, water, heat, metabolite, log_conc) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = ___, values_from = ___)   # which column gives the new column names? which one fills them?

dim(root_wide)

# the numbers only, as a matrix, with the sample names as row names
root_matrix <- root_wide %>%
  select(-sample, -genotype, -water, -heat) %>%
  as.matrix()
rownames(root_matrix) <- root_wide$sample

dim(root_matrix)






NoteCheckpoint



dim() prints two numbers for each table: rows, then columns. root_matrix[1:3, 1:3] shows numbers only, with the sample names as row names.


C2. The PCA.
# scale. = TRUE or FALSE? (see C2 b)
root_pca <- prcomp(root_matrix, scale. = ___)

variance <- round(100 * summary(root_pca)$importance[2, ], 1)
variance
C3. Where are the samples? The PCA never saw water and heat: you only use them now, to colour the points.
root_scores <- as_tibble(root_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(root_wide, sample, genotype, water, heat))

# colour by water regime, shape by heat regime; the variance of each axis in its title
ggplot(root_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = ___, shape = ___)) +

title: 6  Session 6: Genome-wide association: thousands of linear models and one confounder
text:
6.2 Theory (≈45 min)

6.2.1 1. The question: natural variation
Individuals of one species differ, and part of these differences is written in their DNA. A GWAS asks: at which positions of the genome do the individuals with a high value of a trait tend to carry a different letter than those with a low value?
Arabidopsis thaliana is ideal for this. It fertilises itself, so a wild line, an accession, is almost completely homozygous: its seeds are genetically identical to the parent plant. An accession can be sequenced once and grown as many times as needed, in as many conditions as needed. The 1001 Genomes project (2016) sequenced 1,135 accessions and found about 10 million positions where they differ.


6.2.2 2. The data: SNPs coded 0 and 1
A SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) is one position of the genome where some accessions carry one letter and others another, for example A or G. Today’s genotype table keeps more than 20,000 SNPs, about one every 5,000 bases, coded:

0: the accession has the same letter as the reference genome (the lab accession Col-0);
1: it has the other letter.

0 does not mean “normal” and 1 does not mean “mutant”: 0 only means “like Col-0”. Each accession is homozygous, so there are only two values (in humans, who carry two different copies, the coding is 0, 1 or 2).
Only SNPs whose rarer letter is carried by at least 5% of the accessions were kept (the minor allele frequency, MAF ≥ 5%): a letter carried by 3 plants out of 1,000 would be tested on 3 plants only, and one odd plant would be enough to make it look important.
The table has one row per SNP, as in the VCF format used in genomics, and one column per accession. In R, you turn it into a matrix of 0 and 1, as you did with the metabolites in Session 5.


6.2.3 3. One linear model per SNP
For one SNP, the question is the one of Session 4: does the flowering time differ between the plants with allele 0 and those with allele 1?
lm(flowering ~ allele)
The Estimate of allele is the difference between the two means, in days; its p-value says whether the difference is larger than chance. A GWAS repeats this model for every SNP and keeps the p-values: thousands of models, each a fraction of a second.
Many tests. At the 5% level, 1 test in 20 is “significant” by chance alone: with thousands of SNPs, that makes hundreds of false positives, even if no SNP did anything. GWAS use the Bonferroni threshold: 5% divided by the number of tests. Only SNPs below it are called significant. It is stricter than the FDR correction of Session 5 (it controls the risk of even one false positive in the whole genome), and it is the usual choice in GWAS.
The Manhattan plot shows all the tests at once: the position of each SNP along the five chromosomes on the x axis, −log10(p) on the y axis (p = 0.01 becomes 2, 10⁻⁶ becomes 6: high means strong evidence), and a line at the Bonferroni threshold. A real association looks like a tower: not one point, but several neighbouring SNPs raised together, because neighbouring SNPs are inherited together (linkage disequilibrium).


6.2.4 4. Can the scan be trusted? The QQ plot
If no SNP had any effect, the p-values would be spread evenly between 0 and 1. The QQ plot compares the observed p-values (sorted) with these expected ones, both on the −log10 scale:

points on the diagonal, with a few rising at the top right only: a healthy scan, with a few real associations;
the whole curve above the diagonal, almost from the start: too many small p-values everywhere, a sign of a hidden problem.

The inflation factor λ sums up the QQ plot in one number: λ = 1 means no inflation; above about 1.1, be suspicious. It is computed from the median SNP, so a few real peaks do not change it.


6.2.5 5. The confounder: population structure
Plants from the same region share ancestry: over most of the genome, two Swedish accessions are more alike than a Swedish and a Spanish one. Thousands of letters are therefore frequent in Sweden and rare elsewhere, for purely historical reasons. If the trait also differs between regions (say, if the plants of one region flower late), then every SNP with a letter typical of that region looks associated with late flowering. The SNP did nothing: it only tells where the plant comes from. Ancestry is a confounder, like a place on the bench could have been one in the soybean experiment of Session 4, if the plants had not been randomised. In nature, nothing is randomised.
The fix. The PCA of Session 5, run on the genotype matrix (accessions in rows, SNPs in columns), finds the main axes of genetic differences between accessions: they follow ancestry, and geography. Adding the first principal components to every model,
lm(flowering ~ allele + pcs)
changes the question to: among accessions of similar ancestry, do those with allele 1 flower later? This is what adding heat next to water did in Session 4: an effect “adjusted for” another variable. Professionals go one step further with mixed models and a kinship matrix (the genetic similarity of every pair of plants); we stay with the PCs, which you already know.


6.2.6 6. From a peak to a gene
The best SNP of a tower is a marker, not necessarily the cause: it travels with the real cause, which may be another SNP, a deletion, or anything nearby. In Arabidopsis, this travelling together usually fades within about 10,000 bases, so you list the genes within ±20 kb of the best SNP, read what they do, and choose the most plausible one. Databases help: TAIR for Arabidopsis genes, UniProt for proteins (Session 3). A GWAS gives candidates; only experiments (mutants, swapping alleles between plants) prove that a gene causes the difference.
Which plot, for which question?








Your question
Plot or number
In R




Does one SNP change the trait, and by how much?
boxplot by allele, linear model
geom_boxplot(), lm()


Where in the genome are the associations?
Manhattan plot
geom_point() + facet_grid()


Can I trust the scan as a whole?
QQ plot, λ
ppoints(), qchisq()


Do the plants differ by ancestry?
PCA of the genotypes
prcomp()


Which genes sit under a peak?
the gene table, ±20 kb
filter()





6.2.7 7. Worked example: the 1001 Genomes plants

Flowering time (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016): each accession was grown in growth chambers at a constant 10 °C or 16 °C, 16 hours of light, without any winter, 4 plants per accession. The trait is the number of days from sowing to the first open flower (the mean of the 4 plants).
Leaf sodium (Baxter et al., 2010): plants of about 150 of these accessions were grown in the same soil, and the sodium in their leaves measured by mass spectrometry. Too much sodium is toxic for plants: it is the main problem of salty soils.
Genetic groups: the 1001 Genomes project grouped the accessions by ancestry (north_sweden, spain, relict, …); accessions with mixed ancestry are admixed. You will use these groups only to look at the results, never in the GWAS itself.



6.2.8 Practical briefing
Blocks A-E in pairs, block F on your own. Block B meets the plants without any statistics: where they come from, and when they flower. Block C tests two SNPs by hand: one that does nothing, and one that looks important but lies. Block D tests all the SNPs, flowering at 16 °C; block E finds the structure with a PCA, corrects the GWAS, and looks up the gene under the best peak. Block F does the same alone for leaf sodium: same code, a different answer. Your submission is the whole rendered workbook: every block counts.

6.3 Your R toolbox
New tools today, on top of the Session 4 and Session 5 toolboxes (still valid: see the Session 4 R toolbox).

A function and apply()Matrices: rows, columns, t()Manhattan plotQQ plot and λA map


A function packs a few lines of code under a name, so that you can run them again on other data:
snp_p_value <- function(allele) {
  fit <- lm(flowering ~ allele)
  summary(fit)$coefficients["allele", "Pr(>|t|)"]
}

allele is the argument: the data you give the function each time you call it;
the last line is what the function returns: here the p-value of the row allele in the table of coefficients of summary(fit);
flowering is not an argument: the function finds it in your session, so create it first.

apply() runs a function on every row (or column) of a matrix:
apply(genotype_matrix, 1, snp_p_value)   # 1 = each row, 2 = each column
It returns one value per row: here one p-value per SNP, in the order of the rows.
Common mistake. object 'flowering' not found: run the line that creates flowering before apply().









Code
What it does




genotype_matrix["chr1_920099", ]
one row (one SNP), all columns (all accessions)


genotype_matrix[, 1:5]
all rows, the first 5 columns


dim(genotype_matrix)
number of rows, then of columns


t(genotype_matrix)
turns the matrix around: rows become columns


rownames(), colnames()
the names of the rows and of the columns



prcomp() wants the samples (here the accessions) in rows, hence t().


ggplot(gwas, aes(x = position / 1e6, y = -log10(p_value))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(threshold), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(~ chromosome, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x")

position / 1e6: positions in millions of bases (Mb);
facet_grid(~ chromosome, ...): one panel per chromosome, side by side; scales = "free_x" gives each panel its own x axis, space = "free_x" makes each panel as wide as its chromosome is long.



qq <- gwas %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  mutate(expected = -log10(ppoints(n())),
         observed = -log10(p_value))

ppoints(n()) gives n values spread evenly between 0 and 1: the p-values you would expect if no SNP had any effect;
geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) draws the diagonal.

The inflation factor:
median(qchisq(p_values, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
qchisq() turns each p-value back into the test statistic it came from; λ compares the median statistic with the one expected under “no effect”.


world <- map_data("world")
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "grey90", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = accessions, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-12, 90), ylim = c(30, 68))

map_data("world") gives the outlines of the countries (from the package maps);
group = group draws each country as its own shape;
coord_quickmap() keeps the proportions of a map, and xlim/ylim zoom in.

B3. When do they flower? The plants grew at a constant 10 °C or 16 °C, without any winter:

ggplot(accessions, aes(x = reorder(genetic_group, flowering_16C, FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE),
                       y = ___)) +

6.4.4 C. One SNP at a time (15:45-16:10, pairs)
C1. The genotypes.
# one row per SNP (as in a VCF file): its id, chromosome, position, then one column per accession
genotypes <- read_csv("data/arabidopsis_genotypes.csv.gz")
dim(genotypes)
genotypes[1:5, 1:8]   # the first 5 SNPs, the first 5 accessions

7.1 Overview
Download the lecture slides (PDF)
Everybody talks about artificial intelligence (AI). Today you open the box. You start by annotating photos yourself, as thousands of volunteers do for research projects; then you write rules by hand to recognise penguin species, and let a computer learn the same rules from examples. You build a random forest with your own hands, train a small neural network, and compute by hand what the first layer of a deep network does to a camera-trap photo. Finally you read the results of a real deep-learning model trained on amphibians crossing a railway. Then you open the most famous AI of biology, AlphaFold: you download the predicted structure of FLC (the flowering gene of Session 6), read it as a table, judge how much to trust it, and understand how an alignment of related sequences tells AlphaFold which amino acids touch. Finally you explore the AI tools biologists use every day.
Since Session 4 you have used models to explain (does drought change diversity? which SNP is associated with flowering?). Today the goal changes: models that predict, and the one question that matters for them: how good are they on data they have never seen?

A camera trap takes thousands of photos, a microscope thousands of cells, a recorder hours of bird songs. Nobody can look at all of them. What can a machine learn to see for us, how does it learn it, and when should we trust it?

Today nothing is graded and there is nothing to submit. Take your time, try things, ask questions: the goal is that you understand what artificial intelligence does, because you will meet it, use it and judge it during your whole career.

text:
7.3 Theory 1: what is artificial intelligence?

7.3.1 Chihuahua or muffin?
In 2016, the artist Karen Zack posted grids of photos where chihuahuas and blueberry muffins look almost the same: two dark eyes and a nose, or three blueberries. You see the difference in a fraction of a second. Now try to write the rule: “if there are three dark round spots in a triangle, then…”. It does not work: the dog can turn its head, the muffin can have four blueberries, the light changes. Computer-vision services were tested on these grids (Chihuahua or muffin? My search for the best computer vision API, 2017): they mostly succeed, and nobody wrote their rules.
This is the whole idea of machine learning: when we cannot write the rules, we give the computer examples with the right answer, and it finds the rules itself.


7.3.2 AI, machine learning, deep learning








Term
What it means
Example in biology




Artificial intelligence (AI)
Any program that does a task we would call intelligent if a person did it. Includes rules written by people.
An identification key coded as a program.


Machine learning (ML)
AI that learns its rules from examples instead of being programmed with them.
A decision tree that predicts the species from 4 measures (today, block B).


Deep learning (DL)
Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, which also learn what to look at (the features) from raw data: pixels, sounds, sequences.
A network that finds toads in camera-trap photos (block F); AlphaFold.



Each is inside the previous one: all deep learning is machine learning, all machine learning is AI, not the other way round. Generative AI (chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Le Chat; image generators) is deep learning trained to produce text or images rather than to classify them.


7.3.3 The families of learning

Supervised learning: examples come with the answer (the label): photo → “toad”. The model learns to predict the label. Today.
Unsupervised learning: no label; the model finds structure by itself. The PCA and the clustering of Session 5.
Self-supervised learning: the model makes its own labels from the data (hide a word and guess it, hide a piece of a protein sequence and guess it). How chatbots and protein language models are trained.

And the main tasks, all present in the AnnoTrain projects of the instructor:









Task
Question
Output
Example




Classification
Which class?
One label per photo
Animal or not; which amphibian species


Regression
How much?
A number
Age of a fish from a scale; leaf area


Detection
Where are the objects?
A box around each
Each animal in a camera-trap photo


Segmentation
Which pixels belong to what?
A mask
Roots, shoots and seeds on a plate; each cell of a tissue


Tracking
Where does each object go?
A path per individual
Fish swimming in a video


Generation
Produce something new
Text, image, sequence
A chatbot’s answer; a designed protein





7.3.4 The vocabulary of supervised learning

A dataset is a table (or a set of photos), one row per observation (a penguin, a photo).
The features are what the model may look at (the measures, the pixels); the label is what it must predict (the species).
The model is the recipe that turns features into a prediction; its parameters (for a network: its weights) are the numbers it learns. The settings chosen by people before training (the size of a tree, the number of neurons) are hyperparameters.
Training adjusts the parameters so that the predictions match the labels of the training set. A validation set is used to choose hyperparameters and when to stop; a test set, never touched before the end, tells how good the model is.
Inference (or prediction) is using the trained model on new data.

The golden rule, which you already met with the cross-validation of Session 5: a model is only judged on data it has never seen.


7.3.5 Is the model good? The confusion matrix
Rows: the truth. Columns: what the model said. A camera trap, 100 photos, 30 with an animal:









predicted: animal
predicted: empty




true: animal
24 (true positives)
6 (false negatives: missed)


true: empty
4 (false positives: invented)
66 (true negatives)




Accuracy = correct / all = (24 + 66) / 100 = 0.90.
Recall of “animal” = found / all true animals = 24 / 30 = 0.80. Did we miss animals?
Precision of “animal” = right / all called animal = 24 / 28 = 0.86. When it says animal, can we believe it?
The F1 score combines both: 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall).

The accuracy trap. A model that answers “empty” for every photo, without looking, has an accuracy of 70 / 100 = 0.70 here, and a recall of 0 for animals. In real camera-trap projects most photos are empty, and most annotated photos belong to a few common species: always look at the recall of each class, especially the rare ones.

title: 7  Session 7: Artificial intelligence: from rules to machine learning and deep learning
text:
7.4 Theory 2: learning or memorising?

7.4.1 A decision tree
A decision tree asks yes/no questions on the features, one after the other. For three trees of a park, from their leaves: “leaf longer than 12 cm?” → chestnut; otherwise “margin toothed?” → beech if no, hornbeam if yes. To build it, the computer tries every feature and every threshold, and keeps the question that separates the labels best; then it does the same in each half, and so on. It is a dichotomous identification key, but learned from examples. It is easy to read, which is its great strength.


7.4.2 Overfitting
A tree allowed to grow without limit ends with one leaf per training example: it is then 100% right on the training data, by heart. This is overfitting: the model learns the noise and the peculiarities of the training examples instead of a rule that generalises. The signature: very good on the training set, much worse on the test set. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to capture the rule (a tree with one question for three species). You will see it with shuffled labels (as in Session 5): the tree reaches 100% on training labels that mean nothing.


7.4.3 A random forest
One tree is unstable: change a few training examples and it changes. A random forest (Breiman, 2001) grows hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample (the training examples drawn again at random, with replacement) and with a random subset of the features, then lets them vote. Each tree is wrong sometimes, but not on the same examples: the errors cancel out in the majority. It is the same idea as asking several people to annotate the same photo. Random forests are still among the best models for tables of measurements, and the classical pixel classifier of ilastik is one.


7.4.4 A neuron is a linear model
An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a constant, then passes it through an activation function:
\[\text{output} = f(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 + b)\]
The part inside \(f\) is exactly the lm() of Session 4: weights (slopes) and an intercept. The activation \(f\) bends it: ReLU keeps positive values and sets negative ones to 0; the sigmoid squeezes the result between 0 and 1, like a probability. A layer is many neurons side by side; a network stacks layers, the outputs of one being the inputs of the next. With enough neurons, a network can draw any boundary between classes.
Training a network means finding the weights that make the loss (the error between predictions and labels) as small as possible. The algorithm, gradient descent, is a walker in the fog going down a hill: at each step it measures the slope of the loss for each weight and moves the weights a little downhill. One pass over all the training examples is an epoch; a network trains for tens of epochs.

title: 7  Session 7: Artificial intelligence: from rules to machine learning and deep learning
text:
7.5 Theory 3: deep learning for images

7.5.1 A photo is a table of numbers
A grey photo is a matrix: one number per pixel, from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A colour photo is three matrices (red, green, blue). A camera-trap photo of 2,048 × 1,494 pixels is 9 million numbers. A tree asking “is pixel 15,200 brighter than 120?” is useless: the animal can be anywhere, at any size, in any light. What matters are shapes, made by many pixels together.


7.5.2 Before deep learning: features designed by people
Until about 2012, image analysis started with features designed by people: brightness, colour, edges, textures, computed by hand-written formulas, then given to a classifier such as a random forest. It works on simple, well-controlled images (the instructor’s 2025 lecture on root images shows this with ilastik), and fails on the variety of the real world.


7.5.3 Convolution: filters that slide over the photo
A filter (or kernel) is a small grid of numbers, for example 3 × 3. It slides over the photo; at each position, it multiplies the 9 pixels under it by its 9 numbers and adds them up. This is a convolution. With −1 on the left and +1 on the right, the result is large where the photo changes from dark to light: the filter detects vertical edges. You will compute it yourself in block E. Then come ReLU (keep the positive answers) and pooling (keep the largest value of each 2 × 2 square, which halves the size of the image and keeps what was found).
A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a stack of such layers. The key: the numbers of the filters are weights, learned during training. The first layers learn edges and colours, the next ones combine them into textures and corners, the deeper ones into parts (an eye, a leg, a leaf margin) and whole objects. Nobody writes the features any more: they are learned from annotated examples. See them for yourself in the Feature Visualization article.


7.5.4 Why it took off around 2012
Three things came together: data (ImageNet, 14 million annotated photos, built by people annotating online), computing power (graphics cards, GPUs, which do millions of multiplications at once) and better architectures. In 2012 a CNN (AlexNet) won the ImageNet challenge by a large margin; in 2015, ResNet (He et al.) went past 150 layers. The ResNet-18 used by AnnoTrain has 18 layers and about 11 million weights.


7.5.5 Transfer learning: you do not start from zero
Training 11 million weights needs millions of photos. But the first layers of a network trained on ImageNet (edges, textures, shapes) are useful for any photo. Transfer learning (or fine-tuning) starts from such a network and retrains it on a few hundred or thousand annotated photos of your own question. This is how AnnoTrain, Teachable Machine and most biology tools work.


7.5.6 Where the labels come from
A supervised model is only as good as its labels. They come from people: experts, students, volunteers of citizen-science platforms such as Zooniverse or iNaturalist. People make mistakes and disagree, so projects ask several people per photo and keep the consensus (the majority). This “ground truth” is never perfectly true. Two classic traps: class imbalance (a few common species, many rare ones with almost no examples), and domain shift: a model trained on some cameras or some microscopes is often much worse on new ones (Beery et al., 2018).


7.5.7 AnnoTrain
AnnoTrain is the instructor’s open platform that puts the whole chain in one place: a researcher creates a project and shares a link; people annotate (open the link, answer, next photo); the platform builds the consensus, checks the answers (too-fast answers and people who disagree with reference photos do not count), trains a network (ResNet-18 for classification, detectors, U-Net and Cellpose for segmentation), and shows its training curves, its confusion matrix and its mistakes. You can use it for your Master’s project: the goal is to annotate fast, together, and to get a first model without writing code.






NoteThe whole chain



Raw photos → annotation by people → consensus (the labels) → training set / validation set → training (epochs, loss) → evaluation (confusion matrix, recall per class) → model → prediction on new photos → people check the uncertain ones → new labels → a better model.

text:
7.6 Theory 4: AlphaFold, how a structure is predicted

7.6.1 The problem: 50 years old
A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a precise 3D shape, and the shape makes the function: a pocket that binds a molecule, a surface that grips DNA, a pore that lets sodium through. In 1972, Christian Anfinsen received the Nobel Prize for showing that the sequence alone contains the information of the fold. But reading it was another matter: solving one structure by experiment (X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, NMR) takes months to years. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) holds about 200,000 solved structures, while hundreds of millions of protein sequences are known. Since 1994, a blind competition, CASP, asks teams to predict structures that have just been solved but not yet published. In 2020, AlphaFold 2 (Google DeepMind) predicted most of them with an accuracy close to the experiments. In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it (with David Baker, for protein design).


7.6.2 The idea: amino acids that touch evolve together
AlphaFold starts as you did in Session 3: it searches databases for related sequences (hundreds to thousands, from all living beings) and aligns them: a multiple sequence alignment (MSA). Two kinds of information come out of it:

conservation: a position that never changes is probably important (the core of the protein, the active site);
coevolution: if two positions always change together, they are probably in contact in 3D. A positive lysine (K) facing a negative glutamate (E) holds the fold; if a mutation turns the K into an E, the protein unfolds, unless the partner also turns into a K. Over millions of years, such pairs leave a signature of correlated changes in the alignment. You will find one in a small made-up alignment (block G6).



7.6.3 From a sequence to a structure, step by step





flowchart TB
  A["Step 1: Sequence: MGRKKLEIKR... (196 amino acids)"] --> B["Step 2: Search: related sequences (alignment) and known structures"]
  B --> C["Step 3: Evoformer x 48: the alignment table and the pair table talk to each other"]
  C --> D["Step 4: Structure module: the 3D position of every atom"]
  D -- "Step 5: recycling x 3" --> C
  D --> E["Step 6: Output: structure + pLDDT + PAE"]






1. The input is only the sequence of the protein, the letters you met in the FASTA files of Session 1.
2. The search. AlphaFold searches huge databases for related sequences: UniProt, but also billions of sequences read directly from environmental DNA (soils, oceans, guts: metagenomes). It aligns them (a multiple sequence alignment, as with MAFFT in Session 3), often thousands of rows. It also looks for related proteins whose structure was solved by experiment (templates). This step takes most of the computing time of a prediction, before any neural network runs.
3. The Evoformer: two tables that talk to each other. The network keeps two tables and improves them 48 times in a row:

the alignment table: one row per related sequence, one column per position of the protein;
the pair table: one cell for every pair of positions (196 × 196 for FLC), holding the network’s current belief about how these two amino acids sit relative to each other in space. Think of it as the contact map you will draw in G4, but richer.

Each block of the Evoformer uses attention: every position looks at all the others and decides, with learned weights, which ones to listen to, as you would scan a page for the words that matter. Information flows both ways: two columns of the alignment that change together write “probably close” into the pair table (coevolution); the pair table in turn tells the network where to look in the alignment. A special step, the triangle update, checks every trio of amino acids: if A is close to B and B is close to C, then A cannot be 50 Å from C. The network was never taught geometry: it learned these rules from the examples.
4. The structure module. Each amino acid starts as a small rigid triangle (its backbone atoms N, Cα and C) floating at the same point. The module moves and turns every triangle, step by step, until their positions agree with the pair table, then places the side chains. The result: x, y, z coordinates for every atom, the numbers you will read in the PDB file in G1.
5. Recycling. The whole structure is fed back into the Evoformer, and everything runs again, three times: each pass corrects the previous one.
6. The confidence scores. During training, the network also learned to predict its own error: the pLDDT for each amino acid, the PAE for each pair. That is why AlphaFold can say “here, I do not know” (next section).


7.6.4 How it learned
Like everything today, AlphaFold is supervised learning. The examples: about 170,000 structures of the Protein Data Bank solved by experiment, each with its sequence. The label: the experimental 3D structure. The loss: for each amino acid, stand on it, look at all the other atoms, and measure how far they are from where they should be. Two more tricks:

fill in the blanks: some letters of the alignment are hidden, and the network must guess them, exactly like the ___ of your workbook. To guess a hidden letter, it has to understand which positions depend on which: it learns coevolution by itself;
learning from its own best guesses: the first version predicted about 350,000 proteins of unknown structure; the predictions it was very sure of were added to the training examples.

Training took about two weeks on 128 specialised processors (Google TPUs). A prediction then takes minutes to hours: the weights are learned once, and reused for every protein.


7.6.5 Two scores to judge a prediction

The pLDDT (0-100), for each amino acid: how sure AlphaFold is of the local structure. Above 90 very high, 70-90 confident, 50-70 low, below 50 very low. On the website: dark blue, light blue, yellow, orange. A very low pLDDT often means that this part of the protein is really disordered in the cell (it has no fixed shape), which is itself useful information.
The PAE (predicted aligned error), for each pair of amino acids: if the prediction is superposed on the true structure using amino acid A, how far off (in Å) will amino acid B be? Small inside a domain, large between two domains linked by a flexible piece: AlphaFold can be sure of the shape of each domain and unsure of how they sit together.



7.6.6 What AlphaFold 2 does not do

It predicts one chain alone, in one state: no DNA, no ligand, no partner protein, no movement. (AlphaFold 3, 2024, adds complexes with DNA, RNA and small molecules: try the free AlphaFold Server.)
It needs relatives: a protein with few known relatives has a poor alignment, and a poor prediction.
It is not reliable to predict the effect of a single mutation: the prediction of the mutant usually looks like the normal protein.
A prediction is a hypothesis, to be checked with experiments, like a GWAS peak.



7.6.7 See it for yourself
Drag the molecule to turn it, scroll to zoom, hover an amino acid to read its name, position and pLDDT. Try:

FLC, colour “AlphaFold confidence”, style “Cartoon”: the dark blue part is the MADS-box, which grips DNA; the orange tail floats around (switch the colour to “Domains” to check).
RuBisCO, colour “Chemistry”, style “Surface”, then “Cartoon”: a protein that lives in water hides most of its hydrophobic (yellow) amino acids inside, where water cannot reach them; this is what drives folding. In this model, 46% of the buried amino acids are hydrophobic, but only 31% of those at the surface. The yellow patches left outside are a clue: in the chloroplast, 8 large and 8 small RuBisCO chains assemble into one enzyme, and chains often stick to each other by such patches.
HKT1, the same: much more yellow on its surface (41% of its surface amino acids are hydrophobic). It does not live in water but inside the membrane of root cells, surrounded by fatty lipids. Turn it: where would the membrane be?
Any protein, colour “Start to end”: follow the chain from blue to red; the two ends of a chain are often far apart in space.

title: 7  Session 7: Artificial intelligence: from rules to machine learning and deep learning
text:
7.7 Vocabulary







Term
In one sentence




Label
The answer the model must learn to predict (the species).


Feature
What the model looks at to predict (a measure, a pixel).


Training / validation / test set
Data to learn from / to tune and decide when to stop / to judge at the end, never seen before.


Parameter, weight
A number learned during training (a threshold of a tree, a weight of a network).


Hyperparameter
A setting chosen before training (depth of a tree, number of neurons, epochs).


Loss
The error of the model on the training data, which training makes smaller.


Epoch
One pass of training over all the training examples.


Gradient descent
The step-by-step method that moves each weight a little to reduce the loss.


Overfitting
Learning the training examples by heart: good on them, poor on new data.


Underfitting
A model too simple to capture the rule.


Generalisation
Doing well on new data: the real goal.


Confusion matrix
Truth in rows, predictions in columns: where the model is right and how it is wrong.


Accuracy
Share of correct predictions, all classes together.


Recall
Of the true members of a class, the share found.


Precision
Of the predictions of a class, the share that is right.


Class imbalance
Some classes have many more examples than others.


Decision tree
A sequence of yes/no questions on the features, learned from examples.


Random forest
Many trees on random samples, which vote.


Bootstrap
Drawing the examples again at random, with replacement.


Neuron
A weighted sum plus a constant (a linear model), passed through an activation.


Activation (ReLU, sigmoid)
The function that bends the output of a neuron.


Layer, hidden layer
Neurons side by side; hidden = between the input and the output.


Convolution, filter
A small grid of weights that slides over an image and detects a pattern.


Pooling
Shrinking an image by keeping the largest value of each small square.


CNN
A network of convolution layers, for images.


Transfer learning, fine-tuning
Starting from a network trained on other images and retraining it on yours.


Annotation, consensus, ground truth
The labels made by people, the majority answer, and what we take as true.


Inference
Using a trained model on new data.


Domain shift
New data unlike the training data (other cameras, places, microscopes).


Hallucination
A confident but invented answer of a generative model.


Multiple sequence alignment (MSA)
Related sequences aligned position by position (Session 3).


Coevolution
Two positions of a protein that change together during evolution, often because they touch.


pLDDT
AlphaFold’s confidence for each amino acid (0-100).


PAE
AlphaFold’s expected error of position between two amino acids (Å).


Disordered region
A part of a protein without a fixed 3D shape.


Attention
A layer where each position weighs all the others to decide which ones matter.


Template
A related protein whose structure was solved by experiment.


Hydrophobic core
The water-fearing amino acids packed inside a soluble protein.

7.8 Your R toolbox
New tools today, on top of those of Sessions 4-6. rpart and nnet are installed with R: nothing to install.

Train and testA decision treeConfusion matrixA loopA neural networkA structure fileA matrix as an image


Keep the test data aside before training:
train <- my_data %>% filter(split == "train")
test  <- my_data %>% filter(split == "test")


library(rpart)
tree <- rpart(label ~ feature_1 + feature_2, data = train)
tree                          # the questions, as text
plot(tree, margin = 0.1)      # the tree as a figure
text(tree, use.n = TRUE)

predicted <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2) lets a tree grow without limit.


table(truth = test$label, predicted = predicted)   # rows = truth, columns = prediction
mean(predicted == test$label)                       # accuracy
Recall of a class: its diagonal cell divided by the total of its row. Precision: the diagonal cell divided by the total of its column.


A for loop repeats the same lines for each value of i:
for (i in 1:3) {
  print(i * 10)
}
slice_sample(data, prop = 1, replace = TRUE) draws a bootstrap sample; sample(x, 2) draws 2 values of x at random.


library(nnet)
net <- nnet(factor(label) ~ feature_1 + feature_2, data = train, size = 2, maxit = 500)
length(net$wts)                              # number of weights learned
predict(net, test, type = "class")
size is the number of neurons in the hidden layer. Scale the features first (mean 0, standard deviation 1).


A PDB file is a text file with fixed columns: one ATOM line per atom.
lines <- read_lines("data/my_protein.pdb")
ca <- lines[str_starts(lines, "ATOM") & substr(lines, 13, 16) == " CA "]   # alpha carbons
as.numeric(substr(ca, 31, 38))     # x (Å); y is 39-46, z 47-54
as.numeric(substr(ca, 61, 66))     # in AlphaFold files: the pLDDT
as.matrix(dist(coordinates))       # distances between all pairs of points
To download from R, the AlphaFold server wants a browser name: options(HTTPUserAgent = "Mozilla/5.0") first.


m <- matrix(values, nrow = n_rows, byrow = TRUE)   # fill row by row
dim(m)
t(m)                                                # turn by a quarter (transpose)
m[2:4, 5:7]                                         # rows 2 to 4, columns 5 to 7
pmax(m, 0)                                          # negative values set to 0 (ReLU)

7.9 Practical






TipNothing to install



Everything used today comes with R (rpart, nnet) or is already in RStudio Server’s R (tidyverse). The complete workbook renders in about 10 seconds.

In the Terminal tab:

cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_07/data/* ~/bioinfo_course/session_07/data/

This copies everything: the data, your workbook WORKBOOK.qmd (with ___ to fill), the complete workbook WORKBOOK_SOLUTION.qmd, and in solution/ its PDF and plots. You can run these lines again at any time: --update=none never overwrites a WORKBOOK.qmd you have already started.
Then File → New Project → Existing Directory, pick ~/bioinfo_course/session_07, open WORKBOOK.qmd, write your name at the top and click Render once.






NoteCheckpoint



data/ holds ten files: five tables (penguins.csv, camera_trap_pixels.csv, amphibians_history.csv, amphibians_confusion.csv, vegetables_versions.csv), three AlphaFold structures (AF-...-model_v6.pdb), one AlphaFold error file (.json) and toy_alignment.fasta. WORKBOOK.pdf appears; its first chunk lists the columns penguin_id, species, island, bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass, sex, year, split, and counts the penguins per species in train and test.




7.9.2 B. Rules by hand, then rules learned (pairs)
Theory: Theory 1 (vocabulary, confusion matrix) and the decision tree of Theory 2.
The Palmer penguins (Gorman et al., 2014): three species measured at Palmer Station, Antarctica.

B1: plot two measures, and find by eye what separates the species.
B2: write your own rules with case_when(), and measure their accuracy: this is programming before machine learning.
B3: put the test penguins aside, and let rpart() learn the rules from the training penguins. Compare its questions with yours.
B4: predict the test penguins, read the confusion matrix, and compute a recall and a precision by hand.







NoteCheckpoint



The tree has three leaves, one per species, and its questions use two of the four measures. The confusion matrix of B4 is a 3 × 3 table whose numbers add up to the number of test penguins.




7.9.3 C. Learning or memorising? (pairs)
Theory: Theory 2 (overfitting, random forest).

C1: a tree without limit, compared with the small one, on the training and the test penguins.
C2: shuffle the species of the training penguins, and train the same tree: what can it learn?
C3: a random forest built by hand with a for loop: 100 trees, each on a bootstrap sample and two random measures, which vote.







NoteCheckpoint



C1 prints a small table with two rows (small tree, deep tree) and their numbers of leaves, training and test accuracies. C3 prints the votes of 8 trees for 5 penguins (species names), one accuracy for the forest, and a summary of the accuracies of the 100 trees.




7.9.4 D. A small neural network (pairs)
Theory: Theory 2 (a neuron is a linear model).

D1: scale the measures, train a network with 2 hidden neurons, watch the loss fall in the Console, count its weights by hand.
D2: networks of 1, 2, 10 and 100 hidden neurons: more weights, better predictions?







NoteCheckpoint



During D1, the Console prints initial value, a few iter ... value lines, then converged. D2 prints a table of four rows: hidden neurons, weights, training and test accuracy.




7.9.5 E. A photo is a table of numbers (pairs)
Theory: Theory 3 (a photo is numbers, convolution).
A photo from the Caltech Camera Traps dataset (California, CDLA-Permissive licence), in grey levels.

E1: draw the photo from its table of pixels.
E2: three 3 × 3 filters (vertical edges, horizontal edges, blur), applied with a convolution written in R.
E3: filter, ReLU, pooling: one layer of a CNN, computed by hand.







NoteCheckpoint



E1 draws the photo in black and white: a culvert, the ground, and an animal. E2 draws three images of almost the same size, each bringing out different structures. In E3, dim() shows that the image is about half as high and half as wide after the layer.




7.9.6 F. Deep learning for real (pairs)
Theory: Theory 3 (where the labels come from) and the confusion matrix of Theory 1.
A ResNet-18 trained in AnnoTrain to recognise the animals photographed by camera traps along a railway line: mostly amphibians, 10 classes.

F1: its training curves: the loss on the training and validation photos, epoch after epoch.
F2: its confusion matrix, its accuracy and the recall of each species.
F3: three versions of another AnnoTrain model (vegetables), trained on more and more annotated photos.
F4: your own annotations of the beginning of the session.







NoteCheckpoint



F1 draws two curves over 40 epochs. F2 prints one accuracy, a table of 10 classes sorted by their number of photos, and a heatmap with the annotated classes in rows and the predicted ones in columns.




7.9.7 G. AlphaFold: from a sequence to a structure (then after class)
Theory: Theory 4, and its 3D viewer.
FLC (Session 6) has never been solved by experiment: AlphaFold predicted it.

G1, in the Terminal: ask the AlphaFold database about FLC, download its structure, and look inside with the commands of Session 1:

cd ~/bioinfo_course/session_07/data
curl -s https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/Q9S7Q7 | head -c 700
curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o FLC_live.pdb https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/files/AF-Q9S7Q7-F1-model_v6.pdb
head -n 4 FLC_live.pdb
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | head -n 3
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | wc -l
grep "^ATOM" FLC_live.pdb | grep " CA " | wc -l
(-A "Mozilla/5.0" gives a browser name: without it, the server answers 403   Forbidden. If the network fails, the same file is already in data/.)

G2: read the structure as a table in R, and plot the confidence (pLDDT) along the sequence, with the two domains of FLC described in UniProt.
G3: draw the structure from its coordinates, then look at it in 3D: in the viewer of Theory 4 (“See it for yourself”), and by opening your own downloaded file in Mol* Viewer (the viewer of the Protein Data Bank and of AlphaFold DB).
G4: the contact map: which amino acids touch in 3D.
G5: the PAE: how sure AlphaFold is of the position of each domain relative to the other.
G6: how coevolution reveals contacts, on a small made-up alignment.
G7, alone: FLC, the RuBisCO of photosynthesis and HKT1, the sodium transporter of Session 6: which one is predicted best, and why?







NoteCheckpoint



In G1, the first command prints text starting with [{"toolUsed":, and the last one prints the number of amino acids of FLC. G2 draws one line between 0 and 100 over two shaded domains, and counts the amino acids in four bands. G4 and G5 draw two square maps of the same size, with a dark diagonal. G6 finds one pair of positions. G7 prints a table of three proteins.




7.9.8 H. A tour of AI in biology (after class, on your own)
Open at least four of these tools (AlphaFold does not count: you explored it in block G), use each one for real, and fill the table of H1. At least one that identifies a living being.



Tool
What it does
Type of AI




Pl@ntNet
Identifies a plant from a photo (leaf, flower, bark).
Classification (CNN), labels from botanists and citizens


iNaturalist
Suggests the species of any observation; the community confirms (“research grade”).
Classification + human consensus


Merlin Bird ID / BirdNET
Identifies birds from their song: the sound becomes a spectrogram, an image read by a CNN.
Classification of sounds


AlphaFold Protein Structure Database / AlphaFold Server
Block G. Also try the spike of SARS-CoV-2 (P0DTC2) from Session 3, or predict a complex on the Server.

600 million predicted structures of proteins from environmental DNA, by a protein language model.
Self-supervised language model

Segmentation (U-Net style)

Neural network

CNN

Annotate, see the consensus, the models and their mistakes.
Annotation + classification, detection, segmentation

Camera-trap photos sorted automatically: empty or animal, then species.
Detection + classification

Follows the body parts of an animal in a video (behaviour).
Pose estimation


A chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude, Le Chat, Copilot…)
Answers questions, explains and writes code.
Generative AI (large language model)





7.9.9 Using AI well as a biologist

Use an existing tool first. Many questions already have a trained model (Pl@ntNet, BirdNET, MegaDetector, Cellpose, AlphaFold). Train your own (AnnoTrain, Teachable Machine) only when none fits.
Check it on your own data. A model trained elsewhere can fail on your cameras, your region, your microscope (domain shift). Annotate a sample yourself and compute the recall per class before trusting the counts.
Look at more than the accuracy: the confusion matrix, the recall of the rare classes, the photos where the model is unsure.
Report what you used: the tool, its version, its settings, and how you checked it.
Chatbots are excellent assistants and unreliable sources. Ask them to explain an error message or a line of code, to suggest a plot; never trust a number, a reference or a fact without checking it (block G2). They write fluent text even when they invent.
Do not paste unpublished data, personal data, or confidential documents into an online AI: you remain responsible for them.



7.9.10 Wrap-up
Click Render (about 10 seconds) and keep WORKBOOK.pdf: it is your own summary of today, with your answers. There is nothing to submit. Finish block G (AlphaFold) and the tour of block H after class: they are the tools you are most likely to use in your own work.

The complete workbook WORKBOOK_SOLUTION.qmd, with every ___ filled, was copied in block A, with its PDF (code, numbers and written answers) and the plots of each block in solution/. Not there? Download the lecture slides (PDF)
Since Session 3, every practical gave you the question, the data and the steps. In Sessions 8 and 9, you decide. title: 8  Session 8: Group project I: from a dataset to a plan
text:
8.2 Theory (≈30 min)

8.2.1 1. From data to a question
A dataset is not a question. The soybean tables of Sessions 4 and 5 could answer “which bacteria respond to drought?”, “do the two genotypes differ?” or “does the root release other molecules than the leaf contains?”: three different analyses. A good project question is:

biological: it is about organisms, not about the data (“which molecules change?” is a step, “does the plant make protective molecules in the root before the leaf?” is a question);
answerable with these data: the variables it needs are in the table;
focused: one main question, two or three sub-questions at most;
refutable: you can say in advance which result would mean “no”.

A useful exercise: write your question, then the figure that would answer it (axes, colours, panels), then the result you expect on that figure. If you cannot draw the figure, the question is not yet precise enough.


8.2.2 2. The anatomy of a plan
Your PLAN.qmd has seven parts. Each is short:








Part
What to write
Example (the soybean plants of Sessions 4-5)




Question
One sentence, then two or three sub-questions
Does drought change the chemistry of the root more than that of the leaf?


Hypothesis and refutation
What you expect, and the result that would prove you wrong
More molecules change in the root, which meets the dry soil first; refuted if the leaf has as many or more.


Data
Files, rows, the subset you use, how many samples per group
One row per sample and molecule; root and leaf only; 2 genotypes × 4 conditions × 3-4 plants


Variables
Response, explanatory, possible confounders
Response: concentrations; explanatory: drought, organ; other factors to keep in the model: genotype, heatwave


Method, step by step
Each step and the course tool that does it
1. log of the concentrations; 2. PCA per organ (Session 5); 3. one lm() per molecule with FDR (Sessions 5-6) …


First figure
One exploratory figure with a caption, and what it already shows
PC1 vs PC2 of each organ, coloured by condition


Risks and roles
What could go wrong, and who does what
Four plants per group is few; X does the PCA, Y the models …





8.2.3 3. The toolbox: which tool for which question?








If your question is …
Tool
Session




How many, how big, per group?
group_by(), summarise(), count()
4


Is there a difference between groups? Does it depend on a second factor?
lm(y ~ a * b), anova(), boxplot, interaction plot
4


What are the main patterns among many variables? Which samples resemble each other?
prcomp(), heatmap, clustering
5


Which of thousands of features (genes, SNPs, OTUs) are associated with a variable?
one lm() per feature with apply(), Bonferroni or FDR, Manhattan or volcano plot
5, 6


Is an association real, or due to a confounder (ancestry, family, batch)?
add the confounder to lm(), or PCs as covariates
6


Can a variable be predicted from the others, and how well on new data?
decision tree, random forest, train/test split, confusion matrix
7


Is this sequence similar to a known one? How are these genes related?
blastp, mafft, FastTree
3


Where is it?
a map with geom_point() or geom_tile()
4, 6



Two rules. First explore, then test: a plot of the raw data comes before any model. One question, several tools: a good project usually chains three or four of them (for example: exploration, PCA, one model per gene, then a closer look at the best genes).
Your workbooks are your code library. Your files of Sessions 3 to 7 (in ~/bioinfo_course/session_03/ to session_07/) hold working code for every tool of this table. Copy a block that works and adapt it to your tables, rather than starting from an empty chunk.


8.2.4 4. The classic traps
You met each of them in the course; they all come back in real data.

The confounder (Session 6): an association created by a third variable. Accessions from the north flower late and share many alleles; in a lake survey, the fish of the deep station are larger and older.
The batch: samples processed on different days, by different people, in different experiments. Check whether it explains your first PC.
Thousands of tests (Sessions 5-6): with 20,000 genes, 1,000 are “significant” at 5% by chance alone.
Unequal sampling: more observations does not mean more organisms. Ten times more records of a butterfly in 2020 than in 1980 tells you first about the number of observers.
Raw counts are not comparable: a sample sequenced twice as deep has twice as many reads in every gene. Normalise first (counts per million, then a log).
Overfitting (Session 7): a model judged on the data it learned from always looks good. Keep a test set.
Correlation is not causation: the data are observations; say what an experiment would need to show.



8.2.5 5. How you are graded









Points
What counts




Session 8: PLAN.pdf (group)
10
Focused question (2), variables and expected result (2), method step by step with the right tools (3), first figure with caption (2), one difficulty or decision (1)


Session 9: presentation, group part
7 of 10
Question and biological context (1), correct and reproducible analysis (2), clear figures (1), interpretation supported by the results (2), one relevant limitation (1)


Session 9: presentation, individual part
3 of 10
Your own part of the talk: clear, and you master it (1.5); your answer to the instructor’s question (1.5)



The full rubric is on the Session 9 page.
